papers.title: The Negative Drift of a Limit Order Fill
papers.why: Shows that a resting bid is always filled when the price moves against it but only sometimes when it moves in its favour, which costs about half a tick per fill; so the planned post-only buy at the bid will mostly fill in hours where the Up/Down price is falling, the 50% break-even for resting orders is too optimistic, and paper mode should count a fill whenever the book trades through our price and log the result of hours where the order did not fill.

papers.title: Market Simulation under Adverse Selection
papers.why: In backtests, most resting-order fills (roughly 70-90%) were adverse, and simulators that treat fills as independent of price moves badly overstated performance; this is a concrete rule for how the paper engine should model the new resting-order style so paper and live results match.

papers.title: When Do Markets Fully Process Public Information? Evidence from Real-Time Prediction Markets
papers.why: Binary contract prices moved only about 0.64x as far as a public-information fair probability on impact, then kept drifting for several minutes, and the lag was worse in thin books; this gives a ready-made test for our open question (does the Polymarket price at the hour open under-price the reversal the mean-reversion signal predicts?) and suggests logging the price path inside the 120s entry window.

papers.title: Polymarket-v1 Database
papers.why: A free on-chain trade record through 2026-04-28 that includes the 1H Up or Down markets, with the true aggressor side and maker/taker addresses on every trade, so we can check right away whether prices at the hour open lean against the last hour and how resting bids near the open did, without waiting months of paper trading (caveat: the v1 exchange only, and the authors leave Up/Down markets out of their own analysis).

papers.title: The Ghosts of Polymarket: When Off-Chain Matches Meet On-Chain Reverts
papers.why: Matches reported by the Polymarket order book can later fail on-chain, and these reverts were concentrated in crypto Up or Down markets (peaking at 8.5% of daily and over 24% of hourly settlements, around 0.3% after the May 2026 fix), partly from counterparties deliberately voiding trades that turned against them; live mode should confirm fills on-chain before recording a position, and the per-hour record should flag reverted fills so live results stay comparable with paper.

papers.title: Volatility in Prediction Markets: A Structural Approach
papers.why: Models the next-period price move of a binary contract as p(1-p) divided by time left, plus a spread-and-volume term that beats GARCH out of sample on Kalshi (crypto markets included); this gives a cheap baseline for how far the Up price should move during our 120s window, which helps set resting-order fill expectations and suggests spread and volume at the open as context factors.

papers.title: When do prophets profit in prediction markets?
papers.why: Proves that in order-book markets better accuracy does not guarantee profit, that Kelly sizing loses money when forecasts are miscalibrated (as Kronos's confidence is), and that sizing in proportion to (P - ask), buying only above the ask, is the one robust rule; this suggests judging each strategy by Brier score against the market price at entry and reconsidering the fixed 0.05 threshold.

papers.title: Polymarket-v1 Database
papers.why: A free on-chain record of every Polymarket trade up to 2026-04-28, including the hourly Up-or-Down markets, with exact prices and which side was the taker. We can use it to test the open question, whether the price near each hour open already leans against hour H-1, without waiting for live data (only about 3.5 months of it come after the January 2026 crypto fee change).

papers.title: Comparing Sequential Forecasters
papers.why: A way to track, hour by hour, whether Kronos's P(up) or a reversal-adjusted price really scores better than the Polymarket price at the open, and checking often doesn't cause false alarms. In their baseball test it took thousands of games to show one forecaster beat another, so we should expect this to take a long time.

papers.title: When Directional Accuracy Lies: A Base-Rate-Honest Benchmark for LoRA-Adapted TimesFM on Equity Forecasting
papers.why: Says to judge direction calls by how much they beat a trivial rule, using paired tests. For us that means comparing both strategies against always-Up (ties resolve Up, so it wins a bit over 50%) and a simple reversal rule, and checking Kronos's 50 paths for bad tail calibration (they found a nominal 5% quantile covered 44% of outcomes).

papers.title: Forecast Collapse in Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.why: Explains why foundation models give nearly flat, skill-less forecasts on hard-to-predict targets like hourly returns but stay useful on easier ones like volume, which matches Kronos being about 50% on direction while its spread predicts move size. It suggests using Kronos for move size, not direction. By our own math, 50 paths give P(up) a noise of about 0.07 at 50%, bigger than the 0.05 edge threshold.

papers.title: Gaussian-efficient testing by betting on the mean of bounded data
papers.why: The tightest small-sample confidence ranges for a win rate so far, valid even when results aren't independent, plus a version you can check any time. That fits each strategy's hit rate against the 52.25% and 50% break-evens in the results panel, and shows how many bets at about 20 a month it takes to tell a fading 57% edge from noise.

papers.title: When Your Model Stops Working: Anytime-Valid Calibration Monitoring
papers.why: PITMonitor is an open-source detector that flags when a model's calibration changes, keeps false alarms under control even when checked constantly, and estimates when the change happened. Feeding it where each actual hourly close falls among Kronos's sampled paths would catch calibration drift. Their detection took about 77 to 189 samples, a few days of hourly forecasts.

papers.title: Beyond Forecasting: The Belief-to-Trade Layer in Prediction-Market Agents
papers.why: Replays 44 real Polymarket decisions with the forecasts held fixed. A simple 5-point edge filter still lost money (-9.3%), sizing in proportion to edge lost 55%, and quarter-Kelly with selection and exposure caps made +15.9%. The same replay method is a clean way to compare paying the ask against a resting bid, and different sizing rules, on our paper history.

papers.title: Kelly Betting as Bayesian Model Evaluation: A Framework for Time-Updating Probabilistic Forecasts
papers.why: Scores competing probability models by having them Kelly-bet against each other, with each bankroll acting as a credibility score. In simulations with repeated rounds this told a correct 50% model from a wrong 53% one (our edge range) better than average Brier or log loss. That gives a single running Kronos-vs-market score for the per-hour record.

papers.title: When Do Markets Fully Process Public Information? Evidence from Real-Time Prediction Markets
papers.why: On Kalshi binary contracts, prices moved only about 0.64 of what public information implied, moved even less in thin books, and the gap closed over the next few minutes without beating the spread; that gives a ready test design for our untested question of whether Polymarket's price at the hour open already leans against the last hour.

papers.title: Point-in-Time Audit Before Alpha: Public-Archive Availability and a Negative Matched-Budget Study on BTC Perpetual Futures
papers.why: In Binance BTCUSDT perp archives, open interest has no verified publication time plus gaps and out-of-order records, and funding needs an assumed availability delay; every 15- and 60-minute factor kept a positive holdout IC but lost money after costs, so our per-hour context record should log when funding, OI and liquidations were actually available, and our earlier OI/funding filter failures may partly reflect timing noise.

papers.title: Reconciling Open Interest with Traded Volume in Perpetual Swaps
papers.why: Reported BTC perp open interest on Bybit, OKX and Binance often cannot be squared with traded volume at 1-hour intervals, while Kraken is nearly consistent, which argues for logging Kraken futures OI (or running a volume consistency check) before treating OI as a context factor again.

papers.title: Where does the criticality live? Early-warning signals are event-heterogeneous across seven crypto-perpetual liquidation cascades
papers.why: Binance no longer serves historical per-event liquidation data, so our live liquidation feed is the only record and should be stored every hour; funding settles too rarely to warn of anything within a day; and a drop in the variance of the taker buy/sell ratio came before all six BTC cascades where the data existed, making it a candidate warning to watch before fading a flow push.

papers.title: Machine Learning-Based Bitcoin Trading Under Transaction Costs: Evidence From Walk-Forward Forecasting
papers.why: ML forecasts on about 70k hourly BTCUSDT perp bars only survived costs once trades required the forecast to exceed roughly twice the cost; profits clumped in 16 of 27 quarters, and validation loss did not predict test results, which argues for tying Kronos's edge threshold to the fee and expecting uneven per-strategy results.

papers.title: Bitcoin Price Prediction: Peer-Reviewed Evidence and Social Media Discourse
papers.why: Across rigorously tested studies, hourly technical-indicator models did not beat a random walk and daily direction accuracy sat in the low-to-mid 50s, while 1-4h returns showed negative first-order autocorrelation attributed to overreaction and liquidation cascades; that is a realistic yardstick for Kronos and a mechanism to check for the reversal strategy.

papers.title: Stylized Facts of High-Frequency Bitcoin Time Series
papers.why: BTC intraday returns are anti-correlated at short lags, but the short-interval Hurst exponent rose from about 0.42 in 2019-20 to about 0.48 in 2021-22, meaning reversal weakened as the market matured, which is independent support for tracking how fast our flow-reversal edge is decaying.

papers.title: Fragmentation, Price Formation, and Cross-Impact in Bitcoin Markets
papers.why: Across 14 BTC venues, signed trade-flow imbalance was the most useful feature and the Binance and Huobi perpetuals led price formation, but the lead played out in under a second, so at hourly horizons spot vs perp flow is only useful for telling who drove a move (as our perp flow cap does), not as a price lead to trade.

papers.title: Fill-Side Non-Retail Trading on Polymarket: An Empirical Study of Behavioral Tiers and Microstructure Signatures Under Quote-Attribution Constraints
key_findings: Sample: one week, 2026-04-21 to 2026-04-27; 13,356,931 OrderFilled events pulled from the CTFExchange contract on Polygon; 77,204 addresses with at least 5 fills; 43,116 markets (abstract p1; §1.3 p3).

Order placements and cancels happen off-chain in Polymarket's CLOB, so they are absent from both the chain and the PMXT v2 archive. Quote lifetime, quoting intensity and posted spread by address can never be rebuilt from public data. PMXT v2 has only market-level best bid/ask events (Table 1 p11; §5.2 p25).
Density clustering (DBSCAN, 15 configurations) found one cluster and zero noise, so there are no separable trader types. Fallback k-means k=5 had silhouette 0.227 (abstract p1; §1.3 p4).

Tier split: whales (68 addresses, 0.09%) hold $184.2M (28.0%); high-frequency operators (2,952, 3.82%) $154.9M (23.5%); power traders (6,738, 8.73%) $196.8M (29.9%). Together that is 81.4% of notional. Episodic retail is 82.07% of addresses but only 6.8% of notional (Table 2 p17). Mean retail fill is about $4.77 (§1.4 p5).

Descriptive cross-market Spearman correlations: the high-frequency fill cluster's share vs VPIN +0.437, vs two-sidedness −0.366, vs 5-min order imbalance +0.349, vs 60-min persistence −0.201. Its fills concentrate in one-sided, 'toxic', short-horizon mean-reverting markets (Table 6 p24; p25).
20 markets had book mid swings above 10c in short windows; 3,980 addresses are wash-volume candidates (upper bound). Nothing is attributed to specific addresses (§9.8 p38).

Sample is 77.9% sports; crypto is under-represented and short-duration crypto Up/Down markets are not broken out (§1.5 p6; §11.8 p46). Crypto near-resolution activity dispersion of 24.6x vs 0.68x for politics is quoted from a companion paper, not measured here (p3).
papers.evidence_quality: Weak for our purposes. Single week, purely descriptive, no out-of-sample test, no costs, and no breakdown for crypto hourly markets. Many listed analyses are withdrawn or deferred. Venue matches (Polymarket CLOB), but results are dominated by sports. Only the data-availability facts are firm, and they are structural, not statistical.

ideas.idea: Log our own order lifecycle for every hour we trade: signal time, order style, limit price, best bid/ask and top-of-book size at placement, time to first fill, filled size, cancel time at the 120s deadline, and final outcome. Log it for both paper and live. Public data can never show who rested orders or for how long, so our own log is the only way to learn how often a resting post-only bid fills within 120s.
ideas.expected_effect: Makes the upcoming pay-the-ask vs resting-bid choice measurable. Without it, paper-mode fills for resting bids cannot be checked against anything historical.
ideas.citation: 2605.11640 Table 1 p11 (G-QUOTE-LIFE universal fail; G-BOOK market-level best bid/ask only); §5.2 p25

ideas.idea: Test for adverse selection on resting bids. Compare the win rate of signal hours where the resting bid filled with signal hours where it did not (the latter scored on the counterfactual outcome). If filled hours win clearly less often, the 50% maker break-even is misleading and taker entry may net more.
ideas.expected_effect: Could reverse the default order style. The paper's only support is indirect: fast fill-side traders cluster in high-VPIN, one-sided markets, which suggests passive fills happen when flow runs against the resting side.

At decision time, skip or flag the hour if the ask has jumped far from the recent mid (for example, more than 10c within seconds) or sits above the price where our measured hit rate still breaks even after fees.
ideas.expected_effect: Stops us paying a swept or artificial ask on a rare bad book. Expected to trigger very rarely on the usually 1c-wide BTC hourly book.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Kronos already has an implicit cap (P − price ≥ 0.05); Mean Reversion has none.

papers.title: Executable Arbitrage and Market Efficiency in Prediction Markets
key_findings: Main topic is negative-risk multi-outcome markets and the NegRisk Adapter's one-way NO-to-YES conversion, which does not apply to a single binary hourly BTC market (§2.3 p4; §3 p5-6).

L2 CLOB sample (hour-sampled, 14 Apr 2026 to 19 May 2026, from the pmxt Polymarket Orderbook Archive v2): 2,098 positive YES-side violation episodes vs 36 positive NO-side, after taker fees. Median exact durations were 16.15s (YES, n=253) and 7.99s (NO, n=5). 366 of 624 episodes spanned the whole window (Fig 2 p11; §5.2 p11-12).
Historical L2 order-book data exists only from April 2026. The authors rebuilt event-time books from L2 snapshots plus replayed incremental updates (§4.1 p7-8, ref [11]).

WebSocket validation, 8-15 May 2026: across 308,416,666 messages, the YES and NO books were exact mirrors except for 20 isolated API-level mismatches. Apparent same-market YES/NO mispricings are feed-sync artifacts, not tradable arbitrage (Appendix A p19; §7 p16).

Estimated arbitrage profit $1.118M: $1.086M from conversions and $32,283 from settlement baskets. Median profit per conversion fell from about 1 USDC (to Jul 2024) to about 0.20 (late 2024-2025) to about 0.08 (early 2026), consistent with more competition (§5.3 p12-14).

Maker-assisted conversions are more frequent and more often profitable. All-taker conversions are rarer but earn more on average. The weekly all-taker share stayed at or below about 40% from late 2024 through 2025 (p13-14; Fig 5 p22).

Anomaly: 75 conversions by 3 addresses on 2025-12-12, 22:07-22:14 UTC, produced about $381,748 while mids stayed near 50c. The authors read this as thin books temporarily filled with artificial orders and then consumed (§5.3 p13; App D p21-22).

When only midpoints are available, quotes were imputed as a 1c spread at half-cent mids and a 2c spread at whole-cent mids, with a 0.1c adjustment below 3c or above 97c. This is an assumption, not a measurement (§4.4 p10).
papers.evidence_quality: Solid for negRisk arbitrage (259M CLOB trades through Dec 2025; about five weeks of L2 replay with taker fees assumed), but that part does not transfer to our single binary market. The parts that transfer are infrastructure facts: YES/NO book mirroring (7 days, 308M messages, same venue) and when L2 archive coverage starts. The persistence comparison is underpowered (only 5 NO-side episodes), and the FPMM vs CLOB comparison is descriptive, not causal.

ideas.idea: Treat the Up and Down tokens as one book. Build decision prices from one side (Down ask = 1 − Up bid, Down bid = 1 − Up ask). Add a consistency check that logs any mismatch as feed desync, and never let a mismatch create a trade or an apparent arbitrage signal.
ideas.expected_effect: Removes a rare but real source of wrong entry prices or false signals in both paper and live runs; about 20 mismatches per week venue-wide.

ideas.idea: Use the pmxt Polymarket Orderbook Archive v2 (L2 snapshots plus incremental updates, from about April 2026) to backfill hourly BTC Up/Down books at :00-:02 UTC. Two uses: (a) answer our open question by measuring, in cents, how far the Up mid/ask at the open leans against the sign of H-1, for all hours and for Mean Reversion signal hours; (b) replay whether a post-only bid at the best bid would have been traded through within 120s, to get an empirical resting-bid fill rate. First check that hourly BTC markets are covered for every hour, since the paper only used sampled hours.
ideas.expected_effect: Gives about 5 months of history on whether the reversal is already priced in and on maker fill probability, instead of waiting months for forward logs. Directly informs order style and whether the edge survives the market price.
ideas.citation: 2608.00666 §4.1 p7-8 and ref [11] (pmxt archive v2, L2 only from April 2026, snapshot + incremental replay); corroborated by 2605.11640 Table 1 p11 (PMXT v2 carries market-level best bid/ask)

ideas.idea: Wherever a backtest has only midpoint prices (for example, price-history endpoints), impute entry cost with the paper's convention: half-cent mid means a 1c spread, so ask = mid + 0.5c; whole-cent mid means a 2c spread, so ask = mid + 1c. Then add the 0.07·p·(1−p) taker fee. Store the imputed ask separately from any real quote.
ideas.expected_effect: Stops backtests from understating entry cost by 0.5-1c per share, which matters when the break-even is 52.25%.

ideas.idea: When simulating paper fills or pricing past hours, use the order book at decision time, not last-trade prints. On thin books, prints can be manufactured by briefly posted orders.
ideas.expected_effect: Keeps paper results honest and matched to live on rare manipulated or thin-book hours. Small effect on BTC hourly.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Consistent with our 2026-09-14 thin-book finding (books reset at the open with wide spreads) on non-BTC markets.

papers.title: Short-horizon mean reversion in cryptocurrency markets: a matched cross-market measurement
key_findings: Primary test: 15m Binance USDT spot candles, 2025-01-01 to 2026-02-11, 183 pairs vs 187 US stocks/ETFs, strict walk-forward (train 5,760 / test 960). Crypto mean out-of-sample AUC 0.531 (98% of pairs above 0.5; 164/183 FDR-significant) vs stocks 0.499 (5/187). Class gap +0.031 [+0.027,+0.035]; permutation null 4.4 SD, 0 of 340 shifts reach it (§3 p3-4; App B.2 p18).
BTC at 15m: AUC 0.533 [0.527,0.539], n=33,312, coupling A=−0.33, lag-1 return autocorrelation −0.003. Unthresholded BTC accuracy 52.3% (Table 2 p5; §3 p4).

Horizon: focal crypto mean AUC is 0.536 / 0.521 / 0.496 at 15m / 1h / 4h. At 1h, 4 of 4 coins are significant with the constrained model and 3 of 4 with the free model; mean A about −0.13 at 1h and near zero at 4h. At 1h, 58% of 169 crypto pairs stay FDR-significant vs 0% of stocks. 1h walk-forward geometry: 2,160 train / 360 test bars (App C p19; §3 p5; App B.1 p17).

Betting against the previous candle captures most of it: the 1-lag model reaches AUC 0.5267 vs 0.5305 with 12 lags. The gain is +0.0039 [+0.0026,+0.0052] and is complete by 3 lags (Table 6 p17; App A.3).
Reversal is about signs, not size, but grows with move size: the next-bar flip rate rises monotonically across |r_{t-1}| deciles from 50.2% to 53.0% at 15m (§3 p5; Fig 4c).

Flow conditioning (15m, focal coins only): 'flow-driven' bars (taker imbalance same sign as return, about 70% of bars) are followed by reversal that grows with |imbalance| quintile; flow-opposed bars show about 50% flips. Out-of-sample AUC is 0.540 after flow-driven vs 0.519 after flow-opposed; pooled flip-rate gap +0.021 [0.015,0.026] (§5.1 p10-11; Fig 7).
Adding 12 imbalance lags to 12 sign lags adds nothing (0.529 vs 0.529); imbalance alone scores 0.521. Flow acts as a condition, not an extra linear predictor (Table 5 p11).

Things that do not change the reversal: book depth consumed by the move (flip diff −0.002 [−0.007,+0.004]); lagged perp basis terciles (0.533 / 0.537 / 0.536); lagged funding-rate terciles (0.532 / 0.537 / 0.537); trailing volatility terciles (0.536 / 0.539 / 0.534). Hours containing a funding settlement are slightly worse (0.531 vs 0.537). The edge peaks 10:00-14:00 and 21:00 UTC and sags in the Asian morning; UTC session range is 0.531-0.542. The reversal replicates on the perp tape, AUC 0.531-0.538 (§5.1 p11; App D p20; App F p23).

Confidence thresholding: accuracy rises monotonically, reaching 56% on the most confident bars (about 3% coverage) for BTC/ETH at 15m. Gross edge peaks near 1.3bp per trade, below the 5bp maker round-trip on spot; no pair clears it at any threshold; 5m bars are worse (§5.2 p11-12; Fig 8).

Calibration: at btc-1h, only the 3-parameter constrained logit beats the base-rate log-loss (0.6918 vs log 2 = 0.6931). Free AR(12) logit 0.6935, gradient-boosted trees 0.6933 and MLP 0.7005 are all worse than the base rate. Pooled calibration slope is 1.00 [0.95,1.04] constrained vs 0.82 free (App A.5 p17-18).

Decay: frozen six-month holdout (2026-02-12 to 2026-08-08) shrinks the gap from +0.031 to +0.020 [+0.010,+0.028]; 60% of crypto pairs still significant; 77% of the shrinkage is decay on a fixed universe. BTC per-year AUC drifts down mildly; all 24 coin-years 2021-2026 are significant (Table 1 p4; §3 p4-5; App D p20).

Artifacts: labelling up as r>0 (flat = down) inflates reversal AUC; dropping flat bars moves crypto from 0.531 to 0.520. Flat bars are under 1% for focal coins. With both flat-bar and one-bar-gap adjustments, the gap is +0.011 [+0.008,+0.014]. The effect holds on quote-midprice bars (no bid-ask bounce), on Coinbase/OKX/Bybit (all within ±0.002), and on bar grids shifted off the quarter-hour (§2 p2; Table 3 p7; App D p20-21).

Proposed but not run: compare reversal after moves pushed by forced liquidations with reversal after matched ordinary flow-driven moves. Weaker after liquidations would point to an informational story; not weaker would point to liquidity provision (§6 p13).
Conflict of interest: the authors run an automated crypto trading system using a variant of this model with a 15-minute up/down label (Declaration p13).
papers.evidence_quality: Strong on the core fact: strictly out-of-sample walk-forward, large n, joint block bootstrap, exact permutation null, frozen six-month holdout, cross-venue and bounce controls. The venue matches exactly, since Binance BTCUSDT candles are our settlement source. Weaker at our horizon: 1h evidence comes from a 4-coin focal panel plus a population rerun, and all flow, depth, funding and session conditioning was done at 15m only. Costs are spot round-trip bands, not binary-contract pricing, and it never checks whether a prediction market already prices the reversal. Effect sizes are small (1h focal AUC 0.521), and the interval is fit-conditional, so it may be optimistic by a third to a half (App B.1). Authors disclose trading a variant.

ideas.idea: Re-run the paper's flow conditioning on BTC 1h bars in our backtest. For each hour, flag flow-driven (sign(imbalance) = sign(close−open)) vs flow-opposed. Compute the next-hour flip rate by |imbalance| quintile within each group. Check: (a) flow-opposed hours show no reversal, (b) flip rate rises with the quintile, (c) whether plain |imbalance| quintiles reproduce the trailing-168h z threshold (fz > 1.20).
ideas.expected_effect: Checks, or re-scales, the core Mean Reversion filter against an external 15m result (AUC 0.540 vs 0.519; flip gap +0.021). If the dose-response holds at 1h, the threshold can be set from quintiles instead of a tuned z.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Agrees with our flow-push design. The paper never splits spot from perp flow, so our perp fz ≤ 1.24 condition has no outside support. The paper also shows flow adds nothing as a linear predictor (Table 5), so keep flow as a gate or interaction, not an added linear feature.

ideas.idea: Record the size of the H-1 move each hour, normalised by trailing volatility and bucketed into deciles, as a context factor. Test whether the Mean Reversion hit rate rises with move size within signal hours.
ideas.expected_effect: At 15m the flip rate rises steadily with move size (50.2% to 53.0% across deciles). If this holds at 1h, move size could rank signals when the entry price is marginal. CLV captures the candle's shape, not its size.

ideas.idea: Use the liquidation feed to run the paper's untested check at 1h. For each Mean Reversion signal hour, record the share of H-1 volume from same-direction forced liquidations. Compare hit rates for liquidation-heavy vs ordinary flow-driven hours.
ideas.expected_effect: Shows whether liquidation-driven pushes revert more (liquidity provision) or less (informational). Could become a split in the results panel. Needs months of forward data at about 20 signals per month unless historical liquidation data can be sourced.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Partial overlap with the falling-open-interest filter that failed to replicate on ETH/SOL/XRP. Falling OI often coincides with liquidations, so expect a weak or unstable result and read it with that in mind.

ideas.idea: Test whether the reversal is already priced in, using the paper's effect sizes as a guide. Every hour, log the Polymarket Up bid/ask at decision time next to sign(H-1), |r_H-1| and the Mean Reversion signal. Measure the average lean against H-1 in cents for all hours and for signal hours. Our own break-even math: a 57.3% hit rate tolerates a taker ask up to about 55.6c on the bet side (maker fill up to 57.3c). A plain bet against every H-1 (1h focal AUC 0.521; BTC unthresholded accuracy at 15m only 52.3%) likely sits at or below the 52.25% taker break-even even with no lean.
ideas.expected_effect: Tells whether the edge survives the price. A lean of 1-2c removes any unconditional reversal. A lean over about 5c on signal hours would also erase Mean Reversion's taker edge, leaving only maker entry viable.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: None. This is our open question. The authors' disclosed 15m up/down trading system suggests others are harvesting the same sign reversal.
ideas.citation: 2608.21888 App C p19 (1h AUC 0.521, A about −0.13); §3 p4 (BTC 52.3%); Fig 2 p5; Declaration p13

ideas.idea: Benchmark Kronos against the paper's 3-parameter constrained logit on the same 500 unseen BTC 1h hours. Model: P(up) = sigmoid(C + A·Σ_{k=1..N} k^−α·tanh(0.45·r_{t−k}/σ̂)), N=3-12, walk-forward 2,160 train / 360 test. Compare AUC, log-loss vs log 2, and calibration slope. If Kronos does not beat it, fit a simple calibration (Platt or isotonic) to Kronos's P before applying the P − price ≥ 0.05 rule, or record the logit's P as a cross-check factor.
ideas.expected_effect: Shows whether Kronos's reversal-like behaviour is just a noisier, uncalibrated version of a 3-parameter model. The paper finds flexible models (gradient-boosted trees, MLP, free logit) on lagged BTC 1h returns score worse than the base rate. Calibrated probabilities make the price-gap rule meaningful.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Consistent with our Kronos backtest (49-50% direction, uncalibrated confidence, reversal/RSI-like logic).
ideas.citation: 2608.21888 App A.5 p17-18 (btc-1h log-loss: constrained 0.6918, free 0.6935, GBM 0.6933, MLP 0.7005; calibration slope 1.00 vs 0.82); App B.1 p17 (1h geometry); Eq. 1 p2

ideas.idea: Record the constrained-logit P(up) and its gap to the Polymarket ask/bid every hour as a context factor, alongside the planned 'Kronos agreement' factor. This gives a calibrated, price-comparable reversal probability to set against both strategies' bets. It is recorded only and does not gate anything.

papers.title: The Anatomy of a Decentralized Prediction Market: Microstructure Evidence from the Polymarket Order Book (Dubach, v2 May 2026)
key_findings: Data: public Polymarket WebSocket book feed, 2026-02-21 to 2026-04-15 (52 days, 30.3B events, 385,198 markets), joined to 255.4M on-chain OrderFilled events from CTF Exchange V1 over 2026-02-28 to 03-27. The panel is 600 pre-registered markets: the top 100 by volume plus 500 random. Crypto is 348/600 (58%), but there is no breakdown by market type, so nothing is specific to hourly BTC Up/Down (Sec 3-4, p5-6).

Headline measurement result: trade direction inferred from book-feed deltas matches on-chain aggressor side only 59.2% of the time volume-weighted (95% CI 0.542-0.659). Panel mean is 0.615 (CI 0.579-0.653), IQR 0.526-0.681, and the four 7-day window medians are 0.586/0.591/0.618/0.645. Lee-Ready gets about 81% on Nasdaq. The book feed's change_side field says which side of the book moved, not who initiated the trade (Abstract p1; Sec 2.4 p4; Sec 7.1 p12).

Using feed-inferred direction flips the sign of effective half-spread on 67% of comparable markets (16/24) in window A but 50% (15/30) in window B. Kyle's lambda flips on 60% (15/25) vs 43% (13/30). The result is window-specific, and both windows sit at or below chance (Sec 7.2 p12-13).

Ground-truth aggressor side is on chain: takerAssetId==0 means the taker is the buyer, makerAssetId==0 means the taker is the seller. The V1 exchange was replaced by V2 (0xE111180000d2663C0091e4f400237545B87B996B) in April 2026 with a hard cutover; the OrderFilled signature is the same. The last_trade_price feed event was not evaluated (Sec 2.2 p3; Sec 3.1 p5; Sec 7.1 p12).

SF1: median full quoted spread is 400 bps of mid in the 0.4-0.5 and 0.5-0.6 mid bins (184 and 214 markets; IQRs 202-400 and 400-400), which is about 2c at a 50c mid. It widens to 1,339-1,818 bps below 0.20. These are time-averaged across the window (Table 1 p8; Sec 5.1 p7).
SF2: top of book holds a median 13.6% of top-10 depth (p10 2.4%, p90 44.8%). Only 9% of markets have more than half their top-10 depth at L1 (Table 2 p8; Sec 5.2 p7).

SF4: median maker HHI is 0.031 (about 32 effective makers), p90 0.119, max 0.40 (Sec 5.4 p8-9). SF7: self-counterparty wash share median 0.97%, p90 4.5%, max 22.2%; this is a lower bound (Sec 5.7 p10).
SF6: archive ingestion delay has median p50 41.5 ms, p90 166 ms and p99 6,108 ms. The authors say this reflects their collector, not the exchange (Sec 5.6 p9).

Glosten-Harris on the top 100 with on-chain signs: median effective half-spread -0.0003, transitory component 0.00001, adverse-selection component 0.0 (realized spread at a 60 s lag). Tails contain real adverse-selection events plus noise from the 60 s grid (Sec 6 p11-12; Sec 7.4 p14).

SF8: across markets, depth is explained by duration (+0.222), log p(1-p) (-1.02) and log volume (+0.41). Time to close adds nothing (slope 0.008, SE 0.10, n=313). A within-market test was not done (Table 4 p10; p11).
papers.evidence_quality: Strong for the measurement claim: large n, on-chain ground truth, pre-registered panel, replication package. Weak for our purposes otherwise. It is purely descriptive, with no trading returns, costs or fee analysis. Every spread, depth and adverse-selection number is a cross-market median, not specific to hourly BTC Up/Down. Spread measures use a 60 s grid that the authors say is noisy, and sign-flip rates swing about 17 points between windows. It covers only the V1 exchange before April 2026. The 60/40 seller/buyer asymmetry is mentioned only as a caveat and never quantified (Sec 7.4 p14). Use it for measurement hygiene, not as evidence about our market's execution costs.

ideas.idea: If we ever record a Polymarket-side flow factor for the hourly market (net taker buying of Up vs Down, e.g. to test whether the crowd leans against the last hour), never derive buy/sell from order-book deltas. Take aggressor side from trade messages that carry it, or from on-chain OrderFilled on the V2 exchange (takerAssetId==0 = taker bought). Before trusting the trade-message side field, spot-check a sample against on-chain fills, since the paper did not validate last_trade_price.
ideas.expected_effect: Avoids a factor whose direction is right only about 59% of the time. In the paper that noise flipped the sign of a derived measure on 50-67% of markets, enough to reverse a conclusion about crowd leaning.
ideas.citation: 2604.24366 Abstract p1; Sec 2.2 p3 (OrderFilled fields, V1/V2 contracts); Sec 2.4 p4; Sec 7.1 p12; Sec 7.2 p12-13

ideas.idea: Before adopting the resting post-only bid, measure fill-conditional adverse selection in paper trading. For every hour a strategy fires, log both the hypothetical taker fill at the ask and whether a resting bid at the bid would have filled by the 120 s deadline, plus time to fill and Binance spot move since the hour open at the fill moment. Compare win rate and PnL of filled resting orders with taker entries in the same hours, and count missed hours (unfilled resting orders) as lost bets.
ideas.expected_effect: Shows whether the ~1.75c fee saving from resting survives. A resting bid tends to fill when spot has moved against the bet side. If filled resting orders win noticeably less often, or miss disproportionately many winners, paying the ask is better. Do not read the paper's median-zero adverse selection as evidence that resting is safe here: it is a 60 s-lag, cross-market median, and the authors say the tails hold real adverse-selection events.

ideas.idea: Record the book state at the moment each order is sent and filled: best bid, best ask, spread in ticks, size at L1-L3 on the side we hit or join, and the age of the last book update. Compute each bet's break-even from the actual ask paid rather than an assumed 1c-wide book, and make paper fills walk the recorded levels when order size exceeds L1.
ideas.expected_effect: Each extra cent on the ask raises break-even by about 1 point, and the paper's time-averaged median spread near 50c is about 2c, not 1c. Recording the real per-hour spread and depth keeps results panel figures honest and paper fills matched to live. At 5 to a few dozen shares the depth-walk part is probably negligible; the spread part may not be.
ideas.citation: 2604.24366 Table 1 p8 (400 bps median full spread in the 0.4-0.6 bins); Table 2 p8 (L1 median 13.6% of top-10 depth, p10 2.4%)

ideas.idea: Add a stale-book guard at order time. If the last book update for the hourly market is older than a few seconds when the order is priced, refresh the book from REST before sending, and log the book age on every order.
ideas.expected_effect: Prevents pricing against a book that lags a fast BTC minute. The paper's own WebSocket collector had a 6.1 s p99 delay. That figure is about their pipeline, not ours, so this is a cheap safeguard, not a measured problem.

papers.title: Optimal Market Making in Prediction Markets (Feil and Nendel, Jul 2026)
key_findings: Pure theory plus simulation. Price is a martingale probability p = logistic(latent belief). A market maker picks bid/ask to maximize terminal wealth minus a running inventory penalty gamma*q^2*vol^2 and a settlement penalty gamma_T*q^2*p(1-p). The paper proves a unique classical HJB solution and optimal quotes (Sec 2-3, Prop 3.2, Thm 3.3, Thm 3.5).

Order intensity is Lambda = A(t,p)*B(t,p,pi) with exponential decay in quote distance, k(t) rising from 35 to 50, plus boundary factors. The authors state that the empirical form of prediction-market order intensities has not been studied systematically. Parameters are chosen to illustrate qualitative effects, not calibrated to any contract (Sec 4.1 p20; Table 1 p21).

Parameters: T=1 (unitless), sigma0=0.6, sigma1=0.3, sigma2=0.1, eta=3, A0=100, A1=150, xi=2, nu=1, k0=35, k1=50, kappa=1.5, gamma=4e-3, gamma_T=1e-3, Q=100, trade size 10. There are no fees, no tick size and continuous quotes (Table 1 p21).

At zero inventory the optimal spread ranges from about 0.040 to 0.0575 and generally narrows over time. Near settlement it widens for p near 0.5, and at any fixed time it is widest near 0.5 (Fig 1 p23; p24).
Intrinsic skew is zero at p=0.5, positive below 0.5 and negative above. Inventory skew at t=0 spans about ±0.015 for |q| up to 50 and shrinks toward the 0/1 boundaries (Fig 2 p24; Fig 3 p25).

Monte Carlo over 10,000 paths from p0=0.5, optimal vs myopic: mean PnL 12.39 vs 12.47, std 10.34 vs 28.11, mean |q_T| 15.23 vs 49.37, VaR5% 4.20 vs 32.41, ES5% 9.68 vs 40.50. The myopic benchmark runs without the inventory bound (Table 2 p27; Sec 4.4 p25-26, footnote 4).
papers.evidence_quality: No empirical data, no out-of-sample test, no fees or tick grid, illustrative uncalibrated parameters, and a unitless horizon. It solves two-sided liquidity provision with inventory management. We make one directional entry per hour and hold to resolution, so neither the optimal quotes nor the risk-reduction results carry over to our decisions. The only usable piece is the idea of fill intensity decaying exponentially with quote distance, which predates this paper (Avellaneda-Stoikov).

ideas.idea: While running the resting-order test, fit our own fill-probability curve: the probability a post-only Up/Down buy fills within 120 s as a function of distance between our limit price and the Binance-implied fair value at order time (0, 1, 2 ticks), using the exponential form A*exp(-k*distance). The operator then sees an expected fill rate for 'rest at bid' vs 'bid plus one tick' vs 'pay the ask'.
ideas.expected_effect: Turns the order-style choice into a measured fill-rate vs price-improvement trade-off for our market. Use only the functional form; the paper's parameters are explicitly illustrative. This is the same experiment as the resting-order test under 2604.24366, not a separate workstream.
ideas.citation: 2607.17991 Sec 4.1 p20 (intensity form; not empirically studied; parameters illustrative); Table 1 p21

papers.title: Do Prediction Markets Match Option Prices? Bitcoin Threshold Evidence from Binance and Polymarket (Portnaya, Jun 2026)
key_findings: Method: Polymarket 'BTC above K at date T' is matched to a Binance call with the same strike and expiry. Fair value is the cash-or-nothing price e^{-r*tau}*Phi(d2), with implied vol inverted from the Binance option mid at end of each hour. The gap is D = P_poly - P_fair (Sec 2.1 p4; Sec 3.1-3.2 p6; Prop A.1 p15).

Main contract, BTC>$27k end of Sep 2023 (n=214 hourly obs): mean P_poly 0.4043 vs P_fair 0.3484, mean gap +0.0558 (sd 0.1264, t=6.46), HAC CI [0.023, 0.089], mean friction term 0.0427, 41.1% of obs outside the friction band. AR(1) phi=0.849 gives a half-life of 4.2 h; ADF p=0.004 (Table 2 p8).

Pooled over 3 contracts (n=287): mean gap +0.0633, HAC CI [0.033, 0.094]; median 0.064, 68.6% positive. By contract: >$28k Aug +0.0957 (n=37, 100% positive); >$26k Aug +0.0745 (n=36) but HAC CI [-0.027, 0.176], median -0.036 and only 38.9% positive, so not robust (Tables 3-4 p9-10).

Gap drivers (pooled, market fixed effects, R^2=0.221): P_fair coefficient -0.398 (bigger gap at low probability), SE(P_fair) +0.039, time to expiry +0.0008 per hour. Intercept not reported (Table 5 p11).

Delta-hedged proxy backtest: 16 trades, gross PnL 1.649, net 1.113, 69% net win rate, median hold 3.5 h, net alpha 0.067 (p=0.053, HAC CI [-0.008, 0.143]). Numeric fee and spread assumptions for Polymarket and Binance are not reported (Sec 5 p11; Table 6 p12; Sec 3.4 p7).

Vs Deribit the gap is larger: Sep contract +0.1248 (n=645), pooled +0.1105 (n=2,585). ETH 'above $1,700' (Feb-Mar 2023) is mixed: pooled +0.0129 with CI [-0.000, 0.026], three markets slightly negative, one at +0.19 (Table 7 p13; Sec 6.2 p13).

The Polymarket price is the latest trade or quote at or before the Binance hour stamp, so it can be stale; staleness is not quantified. Mapping is 'close but not exact' (oracle vs exchange settlement), and the sample is deliberately narrow (Sec 2.4 p6; Sec 7.1 p13).
papers.evidence_quality: Weak for our venue and horizon. It covers 3 monthly BTC threshold contracts from Aug-Sep 2023, a thin, fee-free Polymarket era, with 287 pooled obs, of which 214 come from one contract. One of the three contracts is not robust, the backtest has 16 trades at p=0.053, the Polymarket series is backward-merged and possibly stale, fee and spread inputs are not disclosed, and ETH is mixed. The gap grows with low probability and long expiry, and our contract at the open is at-the-money with a 1-hour expiry, where both drivers are weakest. Do not carry the 5-11 point magnitude over to us. What does carry over is the method: the digital-option formula gives a spot-based fair value for our contract at any second of the hour.

ideas.idea: Compute a spot-based fair value at the moment each order is priced and at fill: P_fair_up = Phi( ln(S_now/Open) / (sigma_1h*sqrt(tau)) - sigma_1h*sqrt(tau)/2 ), with Open = the Binance BTCUSDT hour open (the strike), S_now = live Binance spot, tau = hours left, and sigma_1h = Kronos forecast spread or trailing hourly realized vol. Use it to (a) re-check the Kronos edge (P - price >= 0.05) against a P shifted by the spot move since the open, not the open-time forecast alone, (b) cap the limit price for both strategies, and (c) log spot move since open and P_fair on every order and fill.
ideas.expected_effect: Our derivation from the paper's formula, not a paper result: a 1-SD BTC move in the first 2 minutes of the hour shifts fair Up value by about 7c (Phi(sqrt(2/58)) ≈ 0.574), and a 30 s move by about 3.7c, whatever the vol level. That exceeds the 5c Kronos threshold and the ~2.25-point break-even margin. Without this, an edge judged at the open can be gone by fill time, and backtest win rates that assume a ~50c entry will not match live fills late in the 120 s window.
ideas.citation: 2606.19517 Sec 2.1 p4 (payoff = digital); Sec 3.1 eq 3.3 p6; Prop A.1 p15

ideas.idea: Answer the open question with a benchmark of 0.50: at the exact hour open, before any spot move, record the Up best bid/ask and mid, then measure mean(Up mid - 0.50) over many hours. Split by (i) direction of hour H-1, (ii) whether the mean-reversion signal fired and which side it bet, and (iii) Kronos's side. With spot at the strike and a 1 h expiry, the option-implied value is about 0.499 plus the tiny ties-Up bonus, so any lean is crowd or market-maker pricing, not fair value. Only count leans of 2 or more ticks as meaningful at the single-hour level.
ideas.expected_effect: If Up is rich by x cents at the open, especially after up hours, then mean-reversion Down bets enter x cents cheaper and Up bets x cents dearer, so direction-specific break-evens differ even though 'both directions work' in the candle backtest. If Polymarket already leans against H-1 by the full edge, the reversal is priced in and the 57.3% hit rate does not translate into PnL at the prices actually paid. The paper's +5.6 to +6.3 point YES premium comes from long-dated, low-probability contracts and predicts little lean for our at-the-money hourly contract, which is why it has to be measured rather than assumed.
ideas.citation: 2606.19517 Table 2 p8; Table 3 p9; Table 5 p11 (gap larger at low P_fair and long expiry); Sec 7.2 p13-14

ideas.idea: Measure how quickly the Polymarket Up mid follows the spot-based fair value inside the entry window. Over the first 120 s of each hour, sample both at 1 s and regress the change in Polymarket mid on lagged changes in fair value (lags 0-10 s), recording the lag and the share of fair-value moves passed through.
ideas.expected_effect: Decides order style and entry timing within the 120 s. If Polymarket lags Binance by seconds, a taker entering right after a spot move toward our side gets a cheaper-than-fair price, while a resting bid gets picked off after moves against us. If pass-through is instant, entry timing inside the window does not matter and the resting-vs-taker choice reduces to fees vs fill rate. The paper's 4.2 h half-life is for monthly contracts in 2023 and says nothing definite about hourly markets in 2026.
ideas.citation: 2606.19517 Table 2 p8 (AR(1) phi 0.849, half-life 4.2 h); Sec 7.2 p13-14 (segmented capital, slow arbitrage)

ideas.idea: In the lean test and in any backtest of entry prices, use the recorded bid/ask at the exact timestamp, never the last traded price carried forward. The paper builds its Polymarket series from trades merged backward to the hour, and that shortcut can manufacture a spurious gap in a moving or thin market.
ideas.expected_effect: Prevents a false 'priced in' or 'not priced in' conclusion caused by stale trade prices, since a trade from 30 s before the open can differ from the live quote by several cents in a fast minute.
