papers.title: The Quarter-Hour Effect: Periodic Algorithmic Trading and Return Predictability in Cryptocurrency Futures (Kim & Hansen, v2 Jul 2026)
key_findings: Data: Binance USDT-margined perpetuals (BTC, ETH, XRP, SOL, DOGE, ADA), aggregate trades in 10-second bars, Jan 1 2021 to Oct 31 2024 (Sec. 2, p.5-7). This is perp data, not BTCUSDT spot, which is what our market settles on.

Bursts at the start of each quarter hour: for BTC, the first 10s of minutes 0/15/30/45 have 1.274x the trades, 1.269x the absolute 10s return and 1.311x the dollar volume of ordinary minutes. Six-asset means are 1.26x, 1.26x and 1.32x (Table A.2, p.48). The top of the hour is the biggest spike (Fig. 1, p.3).

Round-number trade sizes (a sign of human traders) drop most at the top of the hour. For BTC (sizes with 2+ trailing zeros) the drop is -0.20 SD at the top of the hour vs -0.04 SD at ordinary minute starts (Table 2, p.13). The authors read this as heavier algorithmic participation.

One-minute BTC returns are negatively autocorrelated from the minute before each quarter hour (m=14,29,44,59) into the next minute. So minute 59 of hour H-1 tends to partly reverse in minute 0 of hour H. The paper shows this only as a heatmap, with no number (Sec. 4.2, p.17).

Out-of-sample forecast of the 10s return right after each quarter hour (rolling 6-month window, monthly refit, Jul 2021 to Oct 2024, about 117k boundaries per asset). BTC, lagged returns + 28 technical indicators: R2_OOS 3.82%, AUC 0.6035, accuracy 57.30% (Table 3, p.31). Gross return per trade is only 0.375 bp for BTC (0.51 bp mean) vs a 5 bp taker fee (Table A.3, p.52). The authors say it is not a standalone strategy (p.30).

Order imbalance in the first 10s of a quarter hour: its effect on later returns is negative over the first half hour (short reversal), then turns positive and peaks at 8-12h (p.36). BTC slopes are 3.84 / 5.55 / 6.39 bp per unit of imbalance at 4h / 8h / 12h (Table A.4, p.62). BTC imbalance has SD 0.48 and IQR 0.78 (Table A.8, p.66), so the interquartile effect is about 3 bp at 4h. These are full-sample, in-sample fits with R2 of 0.046-0.176% (Table A.10, p.67).

The minute-0 (top of hour) openings add no reliable predictive content beyond the other quarter hours at medium horizons; they add noise (p.34 fn.7; p.72-73). One-minute and five-minute openings show little predictive content (p.36). Dropping the funding-settlement openings (00/08/16 UTC) leaves the result unchanged (Table A.7, p.64).

At 4h, most of the predictive content comes from persistent (lagged) flow: BTC 62%. At 12h the part explained by public price/volume indicators dominates: BTC 64%. The public-signal share rises +45 pp from 4h to 12h, 95% interval [12, 52] (Table 5, p.40; Table A.11, p.68).
papers.evidence_quality: Large samples. The 10s forecast is truly out of sample (walk-forward), but its edge is about 1/13 of a taker fee for BTC, and the authors do not claim tradability. The 4-12h imbalance results are in-sample regressions with HAC/Hodrick errors and a block bootstrap; R2 is under 0.2%, and effects of a few bp are tiny next to an hourly BTC move. Venue is Binance perps, not the spot candle we settle on. No fees in the forecast tests. The phase-dependence pattern was replicated on Bybit (p.19), and the data were independently validated (p.1). Direct transfer to hourly Up/Down direction is weak. What does transfer is the microstructure fact that the first seconds of the hour are the busiest and most volatile, which is exactly when we enter.

ideas.idea: Stop firing orders at t=0 by default. In paper and live, log the BTC spot move from the hour open, the Polymarket Up/Down mid, the spread and the top-of-book size, sampled every second or few seconds over 0-120s. Also log the second-of-hour for every order and fill, both taker and resting. Then choose the submit second (for example after the first ~10s burst) that gives the best average entry price vs fair value and the least adverse resting fills.
ideas.expected_effect: Better entry price and fewer adverse resting fills, size unknown. BTC trades 1.27x more and moves 1.27x more in the first 10s of quarter-hour minutes, with the top of the hour the biggest spike. Our own arithmetic, not the paper's (assumes a 1h BTC SD near 50 bp): a 1 bp spot move shifts fair value at 50c by about 0.8c, so a few seconds of burst can move fair value by more than the 1c spread.
ideas.citation: 2607.09426 Table A.2 p.48; Fig. 1 p.3; Table 2 p.13; implications for liquidity providers p.5

ideas.idea: Record two cheap boundary features each hour, as factors only, not filters: (a) the Binance perp return in minute 59 of hour H-1, and (b) perp order imbalance in the first 10s of minutes :00, :15, :30 and :45 of hour H-1. Check later whether they add anything to the mean-reversion outcome.
ideas.expected_effect: Probably close to zero for 1h direction. The paper finds boundary imbalance reverses only within about 30 min and continues only at 4-12h, with about 3 bp IQR effect at 4h for BTC in-sample. Minute-0 openings add noise. The minute-59 to minute-0 reversal is shown without a size.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Largely repeats the last-15-minute flow filter, which did not help. The paper's funding-settlement check (00/08/16 UTC openings change nothing) fits our finding that the 08:00 UTC expiry effect is small, and its finding that the top of the hour is not special for prediction fits our null time-of-day results. Do not revive those as filters.

papers.title: The Market Maker's Dilemma: Navigating the Fill Probability vs. Post-Fill Returns Trade-Off (Albers, Cucuringu, Howison, Shestopaloff; v2 Nov 2025; v1 titled 'To Make, or to Take')
key_findings: Live experiment on the Binance BTC perp. Continuous quoting Feb 12-19 2024: 232,897 minimum-size maker orders, 127,051 filled. Periodic quoting Aug 21-31 2024: 172,800 orders, 95,998 filled; results 'essentially identical' (Sec. 2, p.9-10). Best-tier fees: taker 1.5 bp, maker -0.5 bp rebate; spread almost always 1 tick (p.10).

Fill probability is easy to predict from queue sizes at posting time. OLS on the binned surface: fill prob = 0.5649 + 0.0159*Q_near + 0.1013*Q_opp - 0.3166*imbalance, R2 0.946 (queues normalized by 99th percentile). Fill prob is about 30% with a large queue on our side and a small opposite queue, and over 90% in the reverse case (p.15). Randomly placed orders in balanced queues fill about 50%, vs under 2% when inferred from other traders' orders (cancellation / signal bias) (p.4).

Fills and later returns move in opposite directions. Orders followed by negative 5s returns are much more likely to fill (Fig. 11, p.20-21). Unconditional maker markout is about -0.8 bp, or -0.3 bp after the rebate (p.20).

Queue position matters (1s markout, before rebate). Large our-side / small opposite queue: front 10% of queue -0.058 bp vs back quartile -0.775 bp. Both queues large: -0.296 vs -1.157 bp. Small our-side queue: position barely matters, -0.539 vs -0.763 bp (Table 1, p.19).

Naive two-sided market making lost almost 60% in about 3 days 7 hours, annualized Sharpe -109, average hold about 11s (p.22). Simple imbalance strategies, net of fees (Table 2, p.24): taker -1.96 bp per round trip on 18,927 trades, despite about +1 bp gross before fees; maker without cancel -0.47 bp; maker with cancel -0.49 bp. The taker results ignore latency (fn.14, p.23).

A profitable maker needs to post against the book imbalance plus a reversal signal. Reversal model: 182,381 high-fill-probability orders, first half of one week for training, second half (about 3.5 days) for testing (p.26, p.30). The balanced-inventory strategy (logistic model, threshold 0.24) made +0.71 bp per round trip, 654 fills/day, Sharpe +11.97, p=0.016. Most other thresholds were negative or insignificant (Table 4, p.31).
papers.evidence_quality: The live, signal-free order data are unusually clean for fill probability and short-horizon adverse selection, and the result held across two runs 6 months apart. Caveats: one venue (Binance BTC perp), minimum-size orders, best-tier fees, horizons of 1-5 seconds, and latency ignored in the imbalance strategies. The reversal model's out-of-sample test is only about 3.5 days, with thresholds scanned on that same test set, so its positive Sharpe is fragile. For us, coefficients and bp numbers do not transfer (Polymarket binary, 1c tick, 120s window, hold to resolution). What transfers is the mechanism: a resting order fills preferentially when price moves against it.

ideas.idea: For every signal in both paper and live, record both outcomes side by side: the taker counterfactual (ask at decision time + 0.07*p*(1-p) fee, held to resolution) and the actual resting-bid attempt (filled or not, fill second, fill price, BTC move from open at fill, final result). Report maker results per signal, not per fill. Compare (i) win rate of filled resting orders, (ii) win rate of unfilled signals (the missed trades), and (iii) the strategy's overall hit rate.
ideas.expected_effect: Filled resting orders should win less often than the signal's overall rate, and missed trades should lean toward winners, because a bid on Up tends to fill after BTC dips below the open. That shrinks the headline 50% break-even advantage of resting orders. The size on Polymarket is unknown; this measures it directly and settles the operator's order-style choice with data.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Contradicts the working assumption that break-even is 50% whenever a resting order fills at its price. That holds only if fills are independent of the outcome, and the paper shows they are not.

ideas.idea: Make paper-mode fills for post-only orders queue-aware. At posting, record the displayed size already resting at our price (queue ahead). Count a fill only after later traded volume at our price exceeds that queue ahead plus our size, or the price trades through our level. Never fill on a touch. Since paper and live share one pipeline, use the same fill model to reconcile live fills against the paper prediction.
ideas.expected_effect: Keeps paper trading from overstating how often resting orders fill and how good those fills are. A touch-based paper fill picks up exactly the favorable no-fill cases the paper shows real makers miss. Without this, paper results for the resting-order option are not comparable to live.
ideas.citation: 2502.18625 Sec. 2 'Alternative forms of data' p.10; Sec. 1.1.1 p.3-4 (signal bias, >95% of maker orders cancelled)

ideas.idea: Queue-position rule for the resting option. If the spread at submit is 2c or wider, post at bid+1c so we start a new queue at the front. If the spread is 1c, a post-only buy can only join the back of the existing bid queue; tag such orders 'back-of-queue' and compare their fill outcomes separately.
ideas.expected_effect: Better post-fill outcomes when books are wide at the open. The paper's back-of-queue fills are 0.4-0.9 bp worse than front-of-queue fills with a large queue on our side, and it recommends posting while the queue is still small. The tag tells us whether 1c-wide hours are structurally the worst case for the resting option.
ideas.citation: 2502.18625 Table 1 p.19; Sec. 5 p.16-19; 'Threading the needle' p.24-25

ideas.idea: When posting, record three numbers: size resting at our bid (queue ahead), size at our side's ask (opposite queue), and the imbalance between them. After a few hundred attempts, fit our own simple fill-probability model on these three. Split filled-order win rates by whether the book leaned against our side at posting.
ideas.expected_effect: Gives a predicted fill probability per hour, so the order-style choice can be made with it. It also tests the paper's point that the only viable resting fills come from posting against book imbalance with a real reversal signal, which our mean-reversion signal is meant to be. Do not reuse the paper's coefficients.

papers.title: When Do Markets Fully Process Public Information? Evidence from Real-Time Prediction Markets (Angelini & De Angelis, Jun 2026)
key_findings: Kalshi NBA winner contracts: 1,438 games, 2,876 contracts, 409,512 contract-minutes of best bid/ask, volume and open interest, Apr 15 2025 to May 25 2026, merged with play-by-play (Table 1, p.6).

Pre-game prices are informative and calibrated. Brier score improves from 0.204 at 24h to 0.199 at close. Calibration slope on the closing price is 0.985. Conditional on the 24h price, the price revision has coefficient 1.292 (SE 0.217), so revisions under-react (Table 2, p.10-11).

Live prices under-react on impact. A one-minute change in an out-of-sample (game-level cross-fitted) win-probability benchmark moves the Kalshi mid only 0.630 (no controls) or 0.638 (controls) for one, n=356,769 (Table 5, p.16). Range across 5 benchmark specs is 0.637-0.698 (Table 9, p.28), and 0.656-0.663 in quote-quality subsamples (Table 10, p.29).
The unabsorbed gap predicts later drift. Raw drift coefficient: 0.150 at 1 min, 0.195 at 5 min, 0.236 at 15 min. Net of later benchmark changes: 0.379, 0.459, 0.484 (Table 6, p.17).

Thin books under-react more: illiquidity +0.0015 per SD. Salient events under-react less: -0.0026. But salience in thin books adds back +0.0014 (Table 7, p.21). Illiquidity does not speed the later correction: gap x illiquidity is -0.022 to -0.037 (Table 8, p.23). In clutch time the response coefficient falls to 0.509 (Table 12, p.31).

Not tradable after the spread. The 5-minute mid return after a gap is +0.39c (all) to +0.87c (|gap| of 200 bp or more). Buying at the ask and exiting at the bid gives -1.20c to -0.36c, negative at every threshold (Table 11, p.30). Exchange fees are not modeled.
papers.evidence_quality: Large panel with an honest out-of-sample benchmark and many robustness checks. But it uses one-minute quotes, and some of the 0.64 may be attenuation from benchmark error, which the drift tests only partly address. The venue is a prediction market with binary payoffs, close to ours, but the information is salient sports events on thinner Kalshi books, not Binance-derived crypto signals that fast bots arbitrage. It shows prices lag public information yet offers no net-of-cost edge (spread only, fees not modeled). Its value to us is a clean method for our untested question and a prior that binary-market prices move the right way but not all the way.

ideas.idea: Answer the open question directly. For past and live hours, pull the Polymarket Up/Down mid and our side's ask at T-10min, T-1min and at decision time. (1) Regress (Up mid - 0.50) at the open on the mean-reversion signal (side and strength of the H-1 push) and on the sign of the H-1 return: does the market already lean against the last hour? (2) Regress the outcome on the open price plus its pre-open revision (T-1min minus T-10min), mirroring the paper's pre-game revision test. (3) Recompute the strategy's PnL at the actual ask plus fee on signal hours instead of assuming 50c.
ideas.expected_effect: Shows whether the 57.3% hit rate turns into money. If the side we bet on already costs about 55c or more on signal hours, the edge over the ask plus fee is gone. The paper's prior is partial pricing at most (0.64-for-one on salient news). Our H-1 flow/CLV features are not salient, so Polymarket may price them less, but this must be measured, not assumed.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: None. This is exactly the untested open question.
ideas.citation: 2606.07811 Table 2 p.11 (calibration slope 0.985, revision 1.292); Table 5 p.16; Sec. 3 eqs. 8-11 p.8

ideas.idea: Log a live fair-value benchmark through the 0-120s entry window: q_t = N(ln(S_t/Open) / (sigma_1h * sqrt(time left in hours))), with sigma from trailing realized vol, sampled at decision time, at submit and at fill, next to the Polymarket mid, ask and spread. Test whether the gap q_t minus mid predicts the Polymarket mid over the next 1-5 min. Split by thin book (spread over 1c or low depth) and by salient hours (large H-1 move in SD units, macro release hours). If a lag exists, use it as an order rule: when spot has moved toward our side and Polymarket lags, pay the ask now; when spot has moved against our side, do not rest a bid.
ideas.expected_effect: Better entry prices, and it avoids resting bids exactly when they would be adversely filled (combine with the 2502.18625 fill logging). Any lag is likely much smaller than Kalshi NBA's 0.64-for-one because BTC hourly markets are watched by bots with Binance feeds. Measure at second resolution; the paper's one-minute numbers are only a prior.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Macro news hours were tried as a direction filter (bigger moves, direction unclear). Here they are only a split for pricing lag and book reliability, not a direction filter.
ideas.citation: 2606.07811 Table 6 p.17; Table 7 p.21; Table 8 p.23; Table 12 p.31

ideas.idea: Score the results panel and every 'priced-in' analysis on executable prices only: ask + fee for taker entries and the actual fill price for resting orders. Never use the mid. Flag hours whose decision-time quote had a spread over 1c or was stale (no book update within N seconds) so they can be excluded or split.
ideas.expected_effect: Prevents mid-price drift from showing up as fake edge; in the paper, positive mid returns turned negative at every threshold once the spread was paid. Our hurdle is lower than the paper's test because we hold to resolution and pay the spread once, not twice, but the fee still applies.
ideas.citation: 2606.07811 Appendix B, Table 11 p.30; p.18

papers.title: Point-in-Time Audit Before Alpha: Public-Archive Availability and a Negative Matched-Budget Study on BTC Perpetual Futures
key_findings: Data: public Binance BTCUSDT USD-M perp archives, 2024-08-01 to 2026-08-01. The original rule (one gap-free 5m grid for trade, mark, index and OI) held for only 304.57 continuous days (87,717 rows). A revised core (trade, mark, index, realized funding; OI switched off) kept 727 complete UTC days, split 436/145/146 days with a 60-min purge and embargo (p2 §1; p4 §3.3; p6 §5.1).

Timing rules: a bar becomes usable at close_time + 1 ms. Funding is assumed usable 5 min after settlement, with 0/5/10/15-min checks that all kept 727 days. OI publication time could not be verified. The OI archive had 9 missing and 3 off-grid records, 1 conflicting duplicate group and 501 out-of-order records. Mark and index were missing all 288 bars on 2026-06-29. Trade klines had no gaps (p3 §3.2; p6 Table 1).

The auditor rejects five known leak types: future shift, same-bar execution, future funding, wrong OI alignment and backward fill. It caught 40/40 injected leaks and wrongly rejected 0/40 legal templates (Wilson 95%: 91.24-100% and 0-8.76%). This only covers known template types (p4 §3.4; p6-7 §5.2, Table 2).

Null controls: 10 paths (5 moving-block label permutations of 15m BTC, 5 synthetic heavy-tailed volatility-clustered paths), 5% missingness, BH-FDR q=0.10. Mean false-pass rate was 0.2910 with no audit, 0.2479 with the basic audit and 0.0625 with the full audit. Paired difference -0.2285 [-0.2595, -0.2012], sign test p=0.00195. Even fully audited legal candidates passed 6.25% of the time on null data. PBO barely moved (-0.001429), and masking gaps was indistinguishable from dropping them (p4 §3.5; p7 §5.3, Table 3).

Search comparison with 1,000 valid candidates per method: qualified candidates were 39 for the adaptive agent, 39 for random search and 29 for tree GP. The agent did not beat random search (p8 Table 4).

One-time historical holdout (146 days; factors on 5m bars with lookbacks of 3-288 bars; 15m and 60m horizons; position = sign of the composite, delayed one bar, non-overlapping). Mean test IC was 0.2352 / 0.1907 / 0.1550, but 0/23 runs had positive net Sharpe at 6 bp taker + 2 bp slippage per side. Median Sharpe -28.04 / -21.16 / -30.11, turnover about 5,158-6,653. 0 of 460 fee/slippage cells (fees 4-10 bp, slippage 1-10 bp) were positive; the best was -5.49. One extra bar of delay also gave 0/23 positive (p5 §3.7; p8 §5.5; p9 Table 5).
Direction accuracy and trade count were not reported, and the main text does not split results by horizon (p6 §4; p10 §7).
papers.evidence_quality: Same underlying data as ours (Binance BTCUSDT perp), including a 60-minute horizon. Costs are included with a sensitivity grid, and the holdout was opened once. But the holdout is retrospective: the protocol was locked after the period ended, so it is not a forward test. Single asset and venue, no external validation. The audit evidence covers known injected leaks only, and intervals are wide. The economic result is for a continuously traded perp paying bp costs with very high turnover, so it does not carry over directly to a once-an-hour binary bet with a fixed fee. Direction accuracy, the metric that matters for us, was not reported. A careful negative-result paper: strong on method, silent on binary hourly direction.

ideas.idea: Check that live inputs match the archive, hour by hour. At each decision, save the exact spot and perp H-1 kline rows used (open, high, low, close, volume, taker buy volume, close time) and the time we fetched them. Each night, download the same candles from data.binance.vision and compare. Count hours where flow push, perp flow push or CLV differ enough to flip whether a bet fires. Also assert that every candle read has close_time + 1 ms <= decision time, and that gaps in the 168h z-score window are left as gaps, not forward-filled.
ideas.expected_effect: No direct accuracy change. It catches the two leak types most likely in a live hourly pipeline (reading an unfinished bar, filling a gap) and shows whether the 57.3% backtest inputs are the same numbers the live bot sees. Any hour where the bet flips becomes a logged event, not a silent divergence.
ideas.citation: 2608.25348 p3 §3.2 (availability = close_time+1ms; no interpolation, backward fill or cross-gap forward fill); p4 §3.4 (same-bar execution and backward fill are audited leak classes); p10 §8 (a file-complete archive is not automatically point-in-time complete)

ideas.idea: Rerun the original BTC 'OI falling' result with OI shifted later in time: +1 and +2 five-minute bars, plus a version stamped by when the data was actually received. If the BTC effect disappears once OI is lagged, it was probably a timing leak. That would explain why it failed to replicate on ETH/SOL/XRP. Apply the same rule to the funding field in the per-hour record (usable at settlement + at least 5 min).
ideas.expected_effect: Settles whether the one-time OI result was real or look-ahead, and sets the timestamp rule for OI and funding in the upcoming context record. Most likely outcome: confirms OI should stay a recorded-only factor.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Repeats a failed filter: OI-falling already failed replication, and funding did not help. This does not revive either. It only checks whether the original BTC result was timing leakage.
ideas.citation: 2608.25348 p3-4 §3.2 (OI publication time unverified; OI disabled as a factor input); p6 Table 1 and §5.1 (9 missing, 3 off-grid, 1 conflicting duplicate group, 501 ordering reversals; funding lag 0/5/10/15 min tested); p10 §7 item 4

ideas.idea: Measure what entry delay costs on Polymarket. For every bet, record best bid and ask at H:00:00, at order send, at fill, and at the 120s deadline. For resting bids, also record whether the fill happened after the Up price moved against us. Report cents lost per 10 s of delay and fill rate by price move. The H:00:00 snapshot also answers the untested question of whether the opening price already leans against the last hour.
ideas.expected_effect: Our candle outcome does not depend on entry time, so delay only changes the price paid. This puts a number on that cost and on adverse selection for resting orders, which directly informs the pay-the-ask vs resting-bid choice. The paper shows a small timing or cost slip can erase a real predictive edge (0/23 runs survived one extra bar of delay).
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Overlaps the planned order-style choice and the open 'is the reversal priced in' question. The paper has no Polymarket or maker-order evidence; it only motivates measuring delay and cost separately from accuracy.
ideas.citation: 2608.25348 p5 §3.7 (position delayed one completed bar; fee/slippage grid); p8 §5.5 (extra one-bar delay: 0/23 positive; positive IC did not imply an economically usable strategy)

ideas.idea: Run a one-off null control on how the mean-reversion thresholds were chosen. Shuffle hourly Up/Down outcomes in moving blocks (for example 24h blocks, keeping volatility clustering), rerun the same grid search and walk-forward that produced 1.20 / 1.24 / 0.80, and record the best walk-forward accuracy under the null over many shuffles. Compare 57.3% to that distribution.
ideas.expected_effect: Shows how much of 57.3% could come from searching over thresholds. For context: n=220 held-out at 57.3% has a 95% interval of about 50.8-63.8%, and its lower end is below the 52.25% taker break-even. The paper found 6.25% of candidates still passed FDR selection on null paths even after a full audit. The result sets realistic expectations for paper-trading outcomes.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Tension with the no-verdicting rule. Use it as a diagnostic that informs expectations, not as a gate that stops paper trading.
ideas.citation: 2608.25348 p4 §3.5 (moving-block label permutations and synthetic volatility-clustered null paths); p7 §5.3 Table 3 (false-pass 0.2910 no audit, 0.0625 full audit; PBO essentially unchanged)

ideas.idea: Keep an append-only log of every filter and factor variant ever tried, including failures (OI, time-of-day, weekday, funding, last-15-min flow, ETH, Monte Carlo, Qlib factors, US open, 08 UTC expiry, macro hours), and of every bucket split the per-strategy panel will show. Display the trial count next to any factor comparison in the panel.
ideas.expected_effect: Stops the upcoming per-hour record from producing false 'findings'. At about 240 bets a year, a 10-point accuracy gap between the two halves of one factor happens by luck about 12% of the time. Across 10 recorded factors, the chance that at least one shows such a gap is about 70%.
ideas.citation: 2608.25348 p2 §1 (append-only candidate accounting); p5 §3.6 (all successful, invalid, duplicate and rejected proposals are kept)

papers.title: Reconciling Open Interest with Traded Volume in Perpetual Swaps
key_findings: Identity: over any interval, the absolute change in OI cannot exceed traded volume. Excess total variation X_TV = max(sum of |ΔOI| over OI updates - volume, 0) is a lower bound on misreporting (p3-4 Eqs 1-6).

Data: tick-by-tick trades, block trades, liquidations and OI pulled directly from exchange APIs, 12 BTC perps on 7 exchanges. Period 1 = Jan 2023, period 2 = Jul-Sep 2023. Proprietary collection (p5 §3, Table 1).

Whole periods: Binance BTCUSDT perp excess was 0 in both. ByBit USDT perp excess was B743,622 ($15.34B) in P1 and B2,012,160 ($56.84B) in P2. OKX USDT perp was B614,661 ($17.36B) in P2 (p6 Tables 2-3).

Share of hours with excess, Binance BTCUSDT perp: 0.4% in P1 and 41.1% in P2. Conditional mean excess per hour: B259 ($5.34M) in P1, B445 ($12.56M) in P2. Per minute: 14.0% then 33.4%. Per day: 0.0% then 27.2% (p7 Tables 4-5).

Share of hours with excess on other venues, P1 then P2: ByBit USDT perp 98.5% / 99.8%; OKX USDT perp 70.8% / 92.7%; Kraken PF_XBTUSD 22.6% / 20.6% (conditional B8-9, about $0.16-0.27M); Kraken PI_XBTUSD 12.0% / 6.4%; HTX USDT perp 0.0% / 0.4% (p7 Tables 4-5).
Kraken and HTX nearly reconcile. ByBit and OKX are 'a category of their own'. Binance, Deribit and BitMEX sit in between. Exchange behavior changed between the two periods (p7 §5; p9-10 §6).

The paper cannot tell whether OI is wrong or volume (liquidations, block trades) is missing. Excess that grows at longer timeframes fits never-reported volume (Binance inverse P2: 48.7% per minute, 83.2% per hour, 88.0% per day). On 2023-08-17 (a >10% BTC drop), Kraken's excess spikes sat at the sharp price moves, consistent with delayed liquidation or OI reports (p8-9 §5).
Kraken's USD perp volume in P2 was $3.03B vs $200.77B for Binance BTCUSDT perp, so Kraken is a small venue (p6 Table 3). The paper does not test whether OI predicts returns.
papers.evidence_quality: Descriptive data-integrity study with no predictive or trading tests and no costs. Tick-level data from direct API connections across 7 exchanges, but only two windows in 2023 (1 month and 3 months), and behavior visibly changed between them, so the numbers may not describe 2026. It cannot say whether OI or volume is the wrong quantity. Peer-reviewed (Ledger vol. 9, 2024). Useful as a warning about the quality of OI and liquidation factors, not as a signal source.

ideas.idea: In the per-hour record, store OI change from both Binance perp and Kraken futures, each with the exchange timestamp and our receipt timestamp. Do not build or read any factor from the sign of Binance's hourly OI change alone. If our OI polling is fine-grained (seconds), also store a consistency flag each hour: sum of |ΔOI| over all updates received minus that hour's perp volume, flagged when positive. When the recorded OI factor is later examined, look at flagged and unflagged hours separately.
ideas.expected_effect: Makes the OI context factor honest about data quality. In Jul-Sep 2023, 41% of Binance BTCUSDT perp hours had OI changes the reported volume could not explain. Caveats: the flag is only a lower bound and will almost never fire at 5-minute polling, so no flag does not mean clean data. Kraken is cleaner but about 1.5% of Binance's volume.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: OI falling already failed as a filter. This does not revive it. It gives one plausible reason (noisy OI on big venues) and a cleaner venue for passive recording only.
ideas.citation: 2310.14973 p3-4 Eqs 1-6; p7 Tables 4-5 (Binance BTC_USDT_P 1H: 0.4% to 41.1%; Kraken BTC_USD_P 22.6% / 20.6%); p9-10 §6 (Kraken and HTX most reconcilable)

ideas.idea: Treat recorded liquidations as a lower bound, not a complete count. Store raw per-venue liquidation events (Binance and Kraken futures) with event and receipt times, not only hourly totals. Never read a 'zero liquidations' hour as truly zero, and cross-check Binance hours against Kraken. Separately, check in Binance's API docs (not these papers) whether its public liquidation stream is sampled or throttled. If it is, hourly notional from it is undercounted by design.
ideas.expected_effect: Prevents the liquidation context factor from being built on an incomplete count that undercounts exactly during fast moves. No accuracy effect by itself.
ideas.citation: 2310.14973 p4 §2 (discrepancy may come from liquidations missing from traded volume); p9 §5 (part or all of liquidations may never be reported; Kraken excess spikes during sharp moves on 2023-08-17 consistent with delayed liquidation reporting)

papers.title: Where does the criticality live? Early-warning signals are event-heterogeneous across seven crypto-perpetual liquidation cascades
key_findings: Seven BTC liquidation cascades on Binance BTCUSDT perp: May 2022, Nov 2022, Aug 2024, Dec 2024, Feb 2025, Apr 2025, Oct 2025. About 2-month windows each, 1m klines (~88,000 bars per event) and 5m metrics (OI, top-trader L/S, global L/S, taker buy/sell ratio), all from the public archive (p3 §2).

Method: detrend the log series with a trailing mean, then take rolling variance and lag-1 autocorrelation. Kendall τ tests the trend over the pre-cascade window. 39 settings per variable (detrend 2-16h, rolling 0.5-4h, pre-window 1-3 days). Onset = the most negative 60-min log return on the crash day; Oct 2025 pinned at 20:50 UTC (p4 §3).

Oct 2025, in-sample: lag-1 autocorrelation was significant in 29/39 settings for taker ratio, 23/39 for OI and 4/39 for price. Aug 2024, out of sample, the pattern inverted: price 28/39, OI 3/39, taker 1/39 (p6 Table 1; p8 Table 2).

All seven events: price shows the signature in 5/7 (0.67-0.85 of settings). It is absent in the two sudden tariff-news shocks, Feb 2025 (0.03) and Oct 2025 (0.10). Feb 2025 shows no precursor in any variable. No variable holds across all events (p7 §4.5; p8 Table 3).
Rising variance does not discriminate: it rises for price and positioning before nearly every cascade and in ordinary regimes too (p5 §4.3; p10 §5).

The only invariant: taker buy/sell ratio variance falls before all 6 events with taker data (median τ -0.13 to -0.44). Against 300 placebo onsets (null centred at zero, P(median τ<0)=0.49), 4 of 6 fall below the 5th percentile. Sign test p≈0.014, Fisher-combined p≈5e-6. Two of six events overlap the null individually, so it is a population-level precursor, not a per-event alarm (p8 §4.6).
Daily long-liquidation notionals 2022-2025 have a Gini of 0.677. On 10 Oct 2025, Binance long liquidations were $1.05B vs about $130M the day before, and intraday OI fell 24.6% (p4 §4.1).
Binance's per-event liquidation archive has been discontinued, so intraday liquidation history is not publicly available. 8-hour funding is too coarse for intraday use (p3 §2).
papers.evidence_quality: Very small sample: 7 events (6 for the taker series), chosen after the fact, one venue. The robustness sweep and cross-event out-of-sample test are good practice. The placebo null is drawn from the same six 2-month files, so the joint p-values are only approximate. Single author. No trading, no costs, and no measurement of hourly direction or returns after onset. Cascades happen roughly twice a year, so any effect on an hourly strategy betting about 20 times a month is necessarily tiny. The strongest takeaways for us are about data availability and 'don't trust single-event signals'.

ideas.idea: Test whether our fades fail when taker flow has gone quiet. At each of the 620 walk-forward decision times, compute the paper's statistic from Binance perp 5m data: Kendall τ of the rolling variance of the detrended log taker buy/sell ratio over the prior 1-3 days (detrend about 4-8h, rolling about 1-2h). Split fade accuracy into terciles of τ. If there is any gap, add τ to the per-hour context record. Our imbalance measure is a monotone transform of the same ratio, and a quiet recent flow variance may also make fz cross 1.20 more easily.
ideas.expected_effect: Likely small or undetectable. The paper's effect is population-level around rare cascades, and at about 200 bets per tercile only gaps of roughly 10 points or more are detectable. Its value is as a tail-risk tag for the moments when fading a one-sided flow push is most dangerous, not as a filter.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Same kind of regime slicing as earlier filters that were too small to judge (time-of-day, US open, 08 UTC). Keep it as a recorded tag, not a gate. Macro news hours already showed bigger moves with unclear direction, consistent with the paper's finding that news shocks carry no precursor at all.
ideas.citation: 2607.27070 p4 §3 (detrend, rolling variance, Kendall τ, 39-config grid); p8 §4.6 (taker-ratio variance falls before all 6 events, 300-onset placebo, 2 of 6 overlap null); p10-11 §5 (population-level only, not a per-event alarm)

ideas.idea: Start saving raw liquidation events now (Binance and Kraken futures, event and receipt times, side, size, price). Binance's historical intraday liquidation archive is discontinued, so the liquidation context factor can only ever be judged from our own recording. Store it as event counts plus notional with a heavy-tail bucket (none / normal / top 1% of hours), not as a smooth average, because liquidations are very concentrated.
ideas.expected_effect: Makes a later look at liquidations as a factor possible at all. Without our own raw record there is no backfill from Binance. The tail bucket reflects the Gini of 0.677 and one day at about 8x the prior day's level. Expect nearly all hours in the low bucket, so any finding will need many months.
ideas.citation: 2607.27070 p3 §2 (liquidationSnapshot dumps discontinued; intraday liquidation microstructure unavailable without commercial data); p4 §4.1 (daily long-liquidation Gini 0.677; $1.05B vs ~$130M prior day)

papers.title: Decomposing Crowd Wisdom: Domain-Specific Calibration Dynamics in Prediction Markets
key_findings: Data: Kalshi has 64.7M trades on 210,608 contracts. Polymarket has 227.6M trades on 116,000 resolved contracts. Both cut off 31 Dec 2025. Calibration is measured by the slope b in logit P(y=1) = a + b*logit(p), using trades priced 5-95c. b>1 means prices are squeezed toward 50%; b<1 means prices are too extreme (Sec 2.3, eq.1, p.4-5).

Kalshi Crypto slopes by time left to resolution: 0.99 (0-1h), 1.01 (1-3h), 1.07 (3-6h), 1.01 (6-12h), 1.01 (12-24h), 1.21 (24-48h), 1.36 (1mo+). Short-horizon crypto prices look calibrated (Table 3, p.5).

The Polymarket Crypto slopes of 1.753 (0-1h) and 1.390 (1-3h) are flagged unreliable. Polymarket timestamps come from block numbers and carry about 3h of noise. Across the reliable bins (3h+) the Polymarket Crypto mean is 1.049 (Sec 2.4 p.5; Table 15 p.22).

Crypto domain intercept is +0.005 (95% CI -0.024 to +0.034), no different from zero. The paper does not report the directional intercept a, which is the term that matters at prices near 50c (Table 6 p.12; Sec 2.3 p.5).
No trade-size effect in Crypto. Large minus single slope is -0.02 on Kalshi and +0.09 (CI -0.16 to +0.36) on Polymarket (Table 4 p.7; Table 17 p.22).
Averaged over all domains, the horizon slope rises from 0.99 within 1h to 1.32 beyond 1 month. The 4-part model explains 87.3% of variance across 216 cells, in-sample (Sec 1.1 p.2; Table 5 p.9).

The Crypto domain mixes many contract types. Kalshi Crypto is 'cryptocurrency price contracts'; Polymarket Crypto is picked by regex on titles and has a 45.0% YES base rate. None of it is split out for hourly Up/Down markets (Sec 2.2 p.4; Table 2 p.5).
papers.evidence_quality: Very large sample, but purely descriptive and in-sample. There is no out-of-sample or time-stability test (the paper lists this as a limitation), and no fees. The Polymarket 0-1h and 1-3h bins, the only ones near our horizon, are unusable because of timestamp noise. Crypto pools many contract types. A slope does nothing to a price at exactly 50c, since logit(0.5)=0, so the headline results barely touch an hourly Up/Down market opening near 50c. The only usable prior is the Kalshi crypto slope of about 1.0 at 0-3h: short-horizon crypto prices are not systematically too squeezed or too extreme, so any edge has to come from our signals, not from generic miscalibration. Relevance is low; the main value is the method.

ideas.idea: Answer our open question with the paper's recalibration regression, extended by one term. On every logged hour (not just signal hours), fit logit P(Up) = a + b*logit(p_open) + c*sign(close_{H-1} - open_{H-1}). Here p_open is the Polymarket Up mid (and separately the Up ask) at the hour open. c<0 with the mid already leaning against H-1 means the reversal is partly priced in. c≈0 with a mid near 50c means it is not. Then restate Hourly Mean Reversion's 57.3% as hit rate minus the average price actually paid for the side it buys.
ideas.expected_effect: Shows whether the 57.3% hit rate is edge over the price paid or partly already in the price. About 720 hours a month gives a usable fit within 1-2 months, far sooner than waiting on ~20 bets a month. The paper's 0-1h crypto slope of about 0.99 suggests b≈1, so the useful terms are a and c.
ideas.citation: 2602.19520 Sec 2.3 eq.(1) p.4; Table 3 p.5 (Kalshi Crypto 0-1h 0.99, 1-3h 1.01); Table 15 p.22 (Polymarket short bins unreliable)

ideas.idea: Before applying the P - price >= 0.05 rule, pass Kronos P(up) through the same logistic recalibration (a + b*logit P), fitted walk-forward on held-out hours. Compare the recalibrated gap with the price, not the raw P.
ideas.expected_effect: With 49-50% direction accuracy and uncalibrated confidence, the fitted b will likely be near 0. The recalibrated P then collapses toward 0.5 and the rule mostly stops firing. That makes the bet count reflect real measured skill instead of raw confidence spread. This borrows the method only; the paper says nothing about models.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: The 500-hour backtest already showed Kronos confidence is not calibrated and direction is 49-50%. This makes that finding part of the entry rule; it does not add skill.
ideas.citation: 2602.19520 Sec 2.3 eq.(1) p.4 (recalibration p* = sigma(b*logit p), Sec 6 implications)

papers.title: The Favorite-Longshot Bias in Prediction Markets: Evidence from Polymarket
key_findings: Data: 588M Polymarket trades by 2.48M wallets, Nov 11 2022 to Mar 29 2026. Return sample is 560.9M purchases, $22.49B. Returns assume holding to resolution, before fees and before maker rebates (Sec 2.2-2.3, Table 1 p.6, p.8).

Longshots (<10c) return -6.30% with each market weighted equally (CI -8.38 to -4.22), -19.35% with dollars pooled (CI -46.99 to +8.30, includes zero), and +4.09% with each parent event weighted equally. Favorites (>=90c) return +0.277%, +0.83%, and +0.392% on the same three weightings (Table 6 p.12).

Across the whole price range (all categories, each market weighted equally), tokens bought in every 5c bin from 4c up to 45c paid off less often than their price. From the 50c bin up to 99c they paid off more often. The confidence interval excludes zero in each bin. The gap peaks at -5.86pp in the 35c bin and +7.28pp in the 60c bin. Returns are worst around 20-25c and best around 60c (Sec 3.3 p.15; Sec 7.1 p.30).

Crypto shows the bias at both ends. Longshots return -14.84% (equal-weighted) and -12.63% (pooled); favorites +0.643% and +0.537%. Crypto is 67.2% of purchases but 25.2% of dollars, with a mean of 1.20 markets per event. No crypto-specific numbers are given for prices near 50c; the Figure 2 crypto curve is visual only (Table 8 p.16; Tables 2-3 p.7; Fig 2 p.18).

Makers (posted buy offers) vs takers (accepted offers), equal-weighted: favorites +0.641% vs -0.460%; longshots -3.50% vs -31.17%. Pooled by dollars the gap mostly disappears: favorites +0.816% vs +0.877%; longshots -17.56% vs -22.17% (Table 9 p.20; Table 16 p.40).

After posted-offer purchases there was no early price drop (the adverse-selection sign the authors looked for). Longshot marks were +3.92%, +16.91%, +7.56% at 5m, 1h, 1d, yet -17.56% at resolution. This was tested only on the tails (Fig 3 p.22; Tables 17-18 p.41-42).

For markets closing within 1 day of purchase, longshot returns are -10.86% pooled and -13.14% equal-weighted (Table 14 p.37). Q1 2026 estimates are provisional because of resolution coverage (App B p.36).
papers.evidence_quality: Huge sample, but descriptive, in-sample, before fees and rebates, and highly sensitive to weighting: the longshot sign flips between weightings, and the maker/taker gap vanishes when pooled. There is no out-of-sample or strategy test. The near-50c result pools all categories and is not broken out for crypto or for hourly Up/Down. In a two-outcome market the 45c and 55c bins are mirror images, so the finding is really 'the side the market favors wins a bit more often than priced'. The tail results (<10c, >=90c) do not apply to us, since we buy near 50c at the open. The maker/taker evidence is tails-only.

ideas.idea: On every entry, for both strategies, record the price paid for the side bought, the complementary token's price, and whether our side was the market favorite (>=50c) or the underdog (<50c) at entry. Report each strategy's hit rate and P&L separately for favorite vs underdog entries. For Hourly Mean Reversion this also shows directly whether the fade side is usually already favored, meaning the reversal is priced in.
ideas.expected_effect: If the paper's near-50c pattern holds in hourly BTC, underdog entries (e.g. a fade bought at 47-49c) will underperform favorite entries at the same hit-rate threshold. The gap could be a few tenths of a point up to several points. With ~20 mean-reversion bets a month a clean split takes many months, so read it alongside the all-hours calibration fit.
ideas.citation: 2609.12878 Sec 3.3 Fig 1 p.15; Sec 7.1 p.30 (4c-45c bins negative, 50c-99c bins positive; -5.86pp at 35c, +7.28pp at 60c); Table 8 p.16 (Crypto two-sided)

ideas.idea: When order style becomes an operator choice, keep shadow records for both styles on every signal hour. Log the ask at decision time (what paying the ask would have cost), whether a post-only bid at the current bid would have filled by the 120s deadline and at what price, and the outcome for filled and unfilled hours alike. Compare net P&L per bet after the 0.07*p*(1-p) taker fee.
ideas.expected_effect: A resting order saves about 1.75c in fees plus about 1c of spread per share, which moves break-even from about 52.25% to 50%. The paper's evidence that posted buys beat accepted offers is weak for our case: it covers tails only, is before fees, and the gap disappears when dollars are pooled. The real unknown is whether fills are adversely selected, i.e. whether resting bids fill mainly when the market moves against us. The shadow records measure exactly that.
ideas.citation: 2609.12878 Table 9 Panel B p.20; Table 16 p.40; Sec 5.2 and Fig 3 p.21-22

papers.title: Settlement Manipulation in Prediction Markets
key_findings: Sample runs Jul 1 2025 to Apr 8 2026. Periods: P1 before these contracts, P2 with 15m and 4h Polymarket BTC Up/Down (Oct 9 2025 to Feb 11 2026), P3 with the 5m contract also live (Feb 12 to Apr 8 2026, 56 days, 16,073 cycles with trades). The 5m, 15m and 4h contracts settle on Chainlink. Per the authors, the one-hour and daily contracts reference a single exchange's spot price directly and are outside their sample (Sec 3.3 p.11; Sec 6.2).

After the 5m launch, in the final 10s before each close, Binance absolute net order flow was 50% higher relative to the rest of the cycle (0.406 log points), absolute return 15% higher (0.140), and depth near the mid 5% higher (0.048). All significant at 1% (Table 2, Sec 6.3.1).

Price reversal after settlement: the first-10s return after the close moves against the final-10s return with slope -0.10 in P3, compared with +0.05 before launch (change -0.152). There is no effect from 20s after the close onward (Table 3).

Near-even cycles (Up price 0.40-0.60 ten seconds before close, about 6% of cycles) show final-10s Binance flow 3.9x that of other cycles (1.37 log), total reversal of about 25%, Binance depth up (+0.17), and Polymarket depth down (-1.02) (Table 4, Table 5, Sec 6.3.2).

The 15m horizon is strongly muted: flow up only 0.068 (vs 0.406 for 5m), no absolute-return effect, no reversal. Near-even 15m cycles (229) show +0.24 flow and no reversal (Tables 6-7, App C.2 Table A3).

The authors label the top decile of a push-intensity score (final-10s |flow| divided by the median |flow| per 10s bin, cutoff 16.11) as 'manipulated': 1,613 cycles. These are 55.7% overnight (21-07 UTC) vs 39.9% for other cycles, 43.6% weekend vs 27.0%, and 18.7% near-even vs 4.4%. When the market favored one side at 90-100%, a push against that side won 34.2% of the time vs 1.0% in other cycles; at 50-60% it won 65.4% vs 41.4% (Tables 8-9).

821 wallets flagged as manipulators (flagged by realized profit, not observed intent) made +$8.22M gross in manipulated cycles and +$0.09M in the rest. Retail lost -$7.61M and was on the losing side in 65.3% of manipulated cycles vs 47.7% of others. Fees not subtracted (Table 10; robust across thresholds, Table A5).

Binance mid vs the Chainlink settlement price: basis -2.45 bps. Binance finishes on the same side of the strike as the actual resolution 84.8% of the time at 5m and 91.3% at 15m; 61% when the move is under 1.8 bps, 100% when it is over about 13 bps. Median absolute 5m return is 6.6 bps (App D Table A4; Table 1).

Theory: a longer horizon makes a fixed-size push pivotal less often, and manipulation profit goes to zero as the horizon grows (Prop 8). A settlement price averaged over many trades is a second defense; a single-instant print is the easiest to move (Sec 5.4). Fee schedules changed several times in the sample. Makers pay no fee and are eligible for rebates funded from taker fees (Sec 6.4.4 footnote).
papers.evidence_quality: Strong design within the 5m period: near-even vs other cycles, before vs after launch, and a 15m placebo, on 16,073 cycles plus full on-chain wallet data. But it is one contract over two months, P&L is gross of fees, manipulators are picked by realized profit, and Binance only partly proxies Chainlink (85% agreement at 5m). Our hourly contract is not studied. The horizon evidence (15m mostly null) implies 1h is much less exposed. The opposite design lever, a single-exchange single-print settlement like our Binance 1h candle close, is only argued in theory. Treat this as a risk to measure, not a documented effect in our market. Every UTC hour boundary is also a 5m and 15m close (and a 4h close every four hours), so the documented final-seconds Binance flow and reversal do appear at our hour boundaries.

ideas.idea: For every settled hour, record from the live Binance feed: final-10s net taker flow, a push-intensity ratio (|final-10s net flow| divided by the median |net flow| per 10s bin within that hour), final-10s return, |close - open| in bps at settlement, and the first-10s return of the next hour. On our positions, flag any bet that won or lost by a margin of a few bps in an hour with a top-decile push ratio. Report the share of P&L decided that way.
ideas.expected_effect: Measures how much of our P&L is decided by final-second prints on a single-print Binance settlement. Hourly moves dwarf the 5m median of 6.6 bps, so few hours should be close enough for a push to decide them; the expected share is small. If it turns out material, the reasonable response is a recorded near-strike-exposure flag, not a new entry filter.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Time-of-day and weekday clustering did not help as filters, and weekend is already recorded. The paper's overnight and weekend concentration (55.7%, 43.6%) should only be read as an interaction with the push ratio, not as another time filter.
ideas.citation: 2606.31675 Sec 3.3 p.11 (1h contract references single exchange); Sec 6.4.1-6.4.3, Tables 8-9; Sec 5.4 (single-instant settlement easiest to push); App D Table A4

ideas.idea: Check whether Hourly Mean Reversion's trigger is partly created by end-of-hour prints. Recompute hour H-1's closing-location value (where the close sits in the high-low range) and its spot flow z-score using H-1 data up to 10s (and 60s) before the close. Split walk-forward signals into those that still pass the CLV*direction > 0.80 and spot fz > 1.20 thresholds and those that pass only because of the final seconds. Compare hit rates.
ideas.expected_effect: The paper shows the final 10s at 5m closes, which include every top of the hour, carry excess flow that reverses by about 10-25% within 10s. That is bp-scale: it can push a close to the hour's extreme but moves the next hour's outcome by well under a point. The likely result is that almost all signals survive. If a meaningful share does not, the 57.3% may partly reflect settlement noise rather than real flow exhaustion.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Partial overlap: last-15-minute flow was tried as a filter and did not help. This is a data-quality check on the last 10-60s, not a new filter, but results should be read with that earlier null in mind.
ideas.citation: 2606.31675 Table 2 and Table 3 (Sec 6.3.1); Table 5 (Sec 6.3.2); Sec 3.3 (5m/15m/4h rolling schedule overlaps on the clock)

ideas.idea: Record entry timing and state around the open: entry timestamp, Polymarket hourly best bid/ask and top-of-book depth, and the Binance move relative to H's open at t = 0, 10, 30, 60 and 120s. Check whether taker entries in the first ~10s get different prices than later ones, and whether resting-bid fills cluster after spot moves against the resting side.
ideas.expected_effect: The top of the hour coincides with 5m/15m settlement, which brings a Binance flow and volatility spike and a first-10s reversal. On the 5m contract, Polymarket depth falls into near-even closes (the hourly book was not measured). If this carries into the hourly book, entry time within the 120s window, and the fill quality of resting orders, could shift effective prices by a fraction of a cent to about a cent. That matters against a ~2.25pp break-even margin. Every hour counts, so a few weeks of data suffices.

ideas.idea: Store the fee rate and any maker rebate per fill from the venue instead of hard-coding 0.07*p*(1-p). Include rebates in resting-order P&L and recompute break-even per trade.
ideas.expected_effect: Keeps the ~52.25% taker vs 50% maker break-even correct if Polymarket changes the crypto fee schedule, which the paper says happened several times in early 2026 (the 5m peak rate went from about 1.56% to about 1.80% at even odds; the paper does not define 'effective rate', so this should not be mapped onto our 0.07 coefficient). It also credits resting orders with any rebate. Small but prevents silent P&L drift.

papers.title: Machine Learning-Based Bitcoin Trading Under Transaction Costs: Evidence From Walk-Forward Forecasting
key_findings: Data and design: Binance BTCUSDT USD-M perp, hourly, 70,872 observations (2018-01 to 2026-01). Rolling walk-forward with 12 months train, 3 months validation, 3 months test, giving 27 quarterly test folds covering 2019-04-01 to 2025-12-31. Target is the next-hour log return (Sec 3.4 p.6; App D Table D.31 p.38).
Hourly log returns: sd 0.7278%, kurtosis above 42, worst hour -20.10%, best hour +16.03% (p.6).

Sign-of-forecast trading without costs looks good: XGBoost long-only 73.50% annual return over 10,619 trades; iTransformer long-short 181.76% (Sharpe 2.78, 17,943 trades). At a flat 10 bps per position change these become -64.00% and -98.62%. Cost drag is 1.43 to 6.06 bps per hour (Table 4 p.16, Table 5 p.16).

Benchmarks: buy-and-hold 56.30% a year, Sharpe 0.82, max drawdown -77.80%. A 24h momentum rule rebalanced hourly loses even before costs in long-short form (-12.04% a year, 5,984 trades) and earns 31.16% long-only. After costs it is -85.06% and -45.93% (Table 4 p.16).

Cost-aware filter: change position only if the predicted return magnitude exceeds lambda × cost × turnover. With lambda=2 and 10 bps, that means a 0.20% forecast to enter or exit long-only and 0.40% to flip long-short (eq.5, Sec 4.1 p.7). Flagship long-only XGBoost goes from -64.00% to 65.40% a year, Sharpe 1.09, trades 10,619 down to 251 (Table 6 p.18).

The filtered strategies do not significantly beat buy-and-hold. Sharpe difference: long-only +0.27 [-0.46, 0.95], Holm p=0.89; long-short -0.19 (Table 8 p.19). Long-short filtered volatility of 63.73% is almost the same as buy-and-hold's 63.83%, so these strategies are mostly just holding BTC (Table 6 p.18).

Results do not rise or fall steadily with lambda. Long-only annual return by lambda: 0.5→35.75%, 1.0→36.17, 1.5→34.31, 2.0→65.40, 2.5→43.18, 3.0→62.77, 4.0→54.56, 5.0→42.83. Long-short is best at lambda=1.0 (62.60%, 252 trades) (Table 16 p.27).
Cost sensitivity for the long-only IR**-best strategy: 0 bps gives 82.51% (5,327 trades), 10 bps gives 65.34% (197), 25 bps gives 34.54% (35) (Table 17 p.29).

Fold stability: 16 of 27 quarters profitable, 14 with positive Sharpe. Median quarter annualised return 7.98%, median 4 trades per quarter, 20 of 27 quarters under 20 trades. 10 quarters had exactly 1 trade, including every quarter from 2024-Q4 onward (Table 18 p.30; Table D.32 p.38).
Validation loss does not predict out-of-sample trading results: Spearman -0.15 to -0.19 (p 0.09 to 0.17, n=81). Using within-fold loss rank instead gives 0.02 to 0.08 (Tables E.33/E.34 p.40).

Adding technical indicators to raw OHLCV helped long-only (73.25% vs 19.96%, Holm-significant with 72h blocks). EGARCH volatility features added nothing robust. The authors note that bigger forecasts clear the filter more often, so feature effects and filter effects cannot be separated (Tables 9-10 p.21).
papers.evidence_quality: Out-of-sample walk-forward over about 6.75 years on the same venue family we settle on (Binance BTCUSDT; perp here, not spot). Costs are a flat 10 bps per position change. There is no spread, book depth, partial fills or maker/taker routing (p.7), so the cost conclusions do not carry over to a binary contract with a price-dependent fee or to resting orders. Weaknesses: the headline lambda=2.0 is also the best result in the test-period lambda grid (possible selection on test data). The positive annual returns look mostly like BTC exposure (many 1-trade quarters; volatility near buy-and-hold). Not significant vs buy-and-hold. Only 251 trades over 6.75 years. Code only on request. The setup holds a continuous position rather than making a binary hour-by-hour bet, so the turnover mechanism does not apply directly to our one-bet-per-hour, hold-to-resolution design.

ideas.idea: Before trusting Kronos's 0.05 edge threshold, group past Kronos decisions by |P(up) - price| (and by the mean predicted return in bps from the 50 paths) and measure the hit rate in each group. The cost-aware filter only adds value if bigger forecasts are more often right, and the paper's own lambda grid shows no steady pattern.
ideas.expected_effect: Shows whether the threshold picks better bets or just fewer bets. Given 49-50% direction and uncalibrated confidence, the likely result is a flat hit rate across groups, meaning the threshold carries no information.

ideas.idea: Account for sampling noise in Kronos's P(up). With 50 paths, the standard error of P near 0.5 is about sqrt(0.25/50) ≈ 7.1 points (our calculation), which is bigger than the 5-point edge threshold. Rerun the 500 unseen hours with 50 vs 500 paths and count how many bets cross the threshold or change side. Then either raise the path count (500 paths ≈ 2.2 pt SE) or require edge > k×SE + fee, and log the SE with each decision.
ideas.expected_effect: Removes bets triggered only by path-sampling noise. Expect a noticeable share of current Kronos bets to disappear or flip at 500 paths.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: 'Monte Carlo randomness' was tried as a filter and did not help. If that test was about Kronos path-sampling noise, this repeats it. If it was the 5m Monte Carlo signal, this is new.

For a resting post-only bid, compare it to the bid with zero fee. Store both 'edge vs ask+fee' and 'edge vs bid' at every decision so the operator's order-style switch changes the hurdle consistently.
ideas.expected_effect: No taker bet will clear the hurdle only against the mid. The recorded pairs show how many signals are viable only as maker orders.
ideas.citation: 2606.00060 eq.5 p.7 (hurdle = lambda × the trade's own cost); Table 17 p.29 (trade count falls 5,327→197→35 as cost goes 0→10→25 bps)

For Hourly Mean Reversion, compare Up-bets to the unconditional Up rate on those hours and Down-bets to the Down rate.

At about 60 Hourly Mean Reversion bets per quarter, the hit-rate standard error is about 6.4 points. So even with a true 57.3% rate, a quarter below 52.25% should happen roughly 1 time in 5 (our normal-approximation calculation).

ideas.citation: 2606.00060 Table 18 p.30 (16/27 quarters profitable, median quarter 7.98%, 20/27 quarters under 20 trades); Table D.32 p.38
