papers.title: Bitcoin Price Prediction: Peer-Reviewed Evidence and Social Media Discourse
key_findings: Survey of 23 retained studies out of about 120 screened, sorted into evidence tiers. The main result is a null: no peer-reviewed study robustly beats the naive baseline across market regimes at 1-6 month horizons (Sec 3.1 p.2-3; App A p.15).

Hourly BTC: Gradojevic et al. 2023 (random forest on technical indicators, expanding window, 2015-2019) find no model significantly beats a random walk at hourly frequency, while daily does (Sec 3.2 p.3; Table 3 p.15). This is consistent with Kronos at 49-50%.

De Nicola 2021 reports significant negative first-order autocorrelation at 1-4h frequency (reversion), attributed to investor overreaction and cascading liquidations. It is in-sample only, 2013-2020, Tier 3, so it shows the mechanism exists, not that it can be traded (Sec 3.2 p.4).

Arain & Snudden 2025 (daily VAR, Oct 2021-Feb 2024): out-of-sample directional accuracy is mostly in the low-to-mid 50s, peaking around 57% for the best predictor. Only 2 of 12 predictors made significant profits, and only during large price swings (Sec 3.1 p.3; Sec 4.2 p.8). Our 57.3% sits at the top of that published range.

Guo et al. 2024: lagged returns of other cryptocurrencies predict a coin's return out-of-sample, with a long-short portfolio still profitable after costs. The survey gives no horizon and no BTC-hourly result (Sec 3.2 p.4). We already tried 'ETH moved the same way' as a filter and it did not help; nothing here justifies reopening it.

Yae & Tian 2022: predictors that work in-sample fail out-of-sample; the best out-of-sample R² for BTC is 2.7% (daily) (Sec 3.1 p.3). McNally 2018's 52% direction on a single split is within noise (Sec 3.4 p.5).

Proposed minimum standards: walk-forward testing, at least 3 non-overlapping holdout windows in different regimes, a naive-baseline comparison, a 'no change' option in every tuning grid, Diebold-Mariano / Model Confidence Set tests, reporting how many configurations were tried (Bailey et al. 2014), and computing all preprocessing statistics from the training window only (Sec 7 p.10-11).
papers.evidence_quality: A narrative survey: no new data, no new tests, one author, AI-assisted (App B p.16). The social media section is illustrative only. The hourly evidence is second-hand and dated: Gradojevic ends 2019, and De Nicola is in-sample only. The survey gives no venue, fee or cost details for sub-daily results. Its value to us is the evaluation checklist and two pointers (hourly model forecasts do not beat a random walk; 1-4h reversal is linked to liquidations), not effect sizes.

ideas.idea: Treat the Polymarket open price as the baseline Kronos must beat. On the same hours, compute Brier score and log loss for Kronos P(up) and for the Polymarket mid, run a Diebold-Mariano test on the per-hour loss difference, and also score a 50/50 blend of the two.
ideas.expected_effect: Directly measures whether Kronos adds anything beyond the market price. Given 49-50% direction, the likely result is that it adds nothing, which would also tell us whether 'Kronos agreement' is worth recording as a factor.
ideas.citation: 2606.00071 Sec 7 recs 3 and 5 p.11; Table 1 p.2 (naive baseline for direction classification)

ideas.idea: Answer the open question with the market as baseline. Across all hours, regress the Up mid at the hour open on sign(H-1 return) and on the Hourly Mean Reversion signal. For each Hourly Mean Reversion bet, record the entry price of the side taken, and report hit rate minus average price paid instead of hit rate minus 50%.
ideas.expected_effect: If the market already leans X cents against hour H-1 when the signal fires, the real edge is about 7.3 - X points rather than 7.3. That decides whether pay-the-ask is viable at all and how much the maker option matters.
ideas.citation: 2606.00071 Sec 7 recs 3 and 6 p.11 (compare to the naive baseline; check economic, not just statistical, significance)

ideas.idea: Report Hourly Mean Reversion's held-out result against each order style's break-even, and log how many configurations were ever tried. Held-out n=220 at 57.3% gives SE ≈ 3.3 pts: z ≈ 2.2 vs 50% (one-sided p ≈ 0.014) but only z ≈ 1.5 vs 52.25% (p ≈ 0.065) (our calculation). Tried so far: three tuned thresholds plus at least 9 rejected filters. Show a multiple-testing-adjusted interval in the results panel.
ideas.expected_effect: Makes clear the held-out edge is significant at the maker break-even but not at the taker break-even. That bears directly on the upcoming pay-the-ask vs resting-bid choice.
ideas.citation: 2606.00071 Sec 3.4 p.6 and Sec 7 recs 5 and 8 p.11 (Bailey et al. 2014 backtest overfitting); Sec 4.2 p.8 (best published out-of-sample direction about 57%)

ideas.idea: Rerun the Hourly Mean Reversion walk-forward with each condition's 'off' setting as a candidate in every window (no perp-flow condition, no CLV condition, different spot fz cut-offs), and report results in at least 3 non-overlapping regime windows (for example the 2022 bear, the 2023 range and the 2024-25 bull) instead of one pooled number.
ideas.expected_effect: Shows whether the perp and CLV conditions actually earn their place or were fitted, and which regime the 2.4 pts/yr decay comes from.

ideas.idea: Split Hourly Mean Reversion bets (walk-forward and live paper) by whether hour H-1 had heavy Binance liquidations in the direction of the move (liquidation volume z-score vs trailing 168h above a fixed cut-off), and compare hit rates.
ideas.expected_effect: If De Nicola's mechanism holds, liquidation-driven pushes should revert more often. Expect a small difference at most, since the source is in-sample only.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Repeats a factor already planned: liquidations are on the upcoming per-hour record list. This paper only adds a reason to split on it, not new evidence.
ideas.citation: 2606.00071 Sec 3.2 p.4 (De Nicola 2021, 1-4h negative autocorrelation linked to cascading liquidations)

papers.title: Stylized Facts of High-Frequency Bitcoin Time Series
key_findings: Data: Reuters Datascope BTC/USD at 10-minute frequency. Period 1 runs 2019-04-02 to 2020-12-31; Period 2 runs 2021-01-01 to 2022-05-09. Earlier data excluded as spurious (Sec 5 p.8). Returns are simple USD price differences, not log returns (Eq.1 and Eq.4 p.5).

Scaling from the peak of the return distribution: over short intervals H=0.415±0.006 (Period 1) and 0.478±0.004 (Period 2), meaning anti-persistent. Over long intervals H=0.610±0.007 and 0.646±0.004 (Sec 5.1 p.9). The discussion calls this trending 'up to 5 hours' (Sec 6 p.20). The exact crossover interval is not given.
Short-horizon anti-persistence moved toward random-walk behaviour between periods (H ~0.42 to ~0.49), which the authors read as the market becoming more efficient (abstract p.1).

The autocorrelation of 10-minute returns is negative at short lags and oscillates around zero from 30 to 200 minutes (about 2.5h). Lags under 20 minutes are attributed to microstructure (Sec 5.2 p.13; Sec 6 p.20-21). This is roughly in line with our finding that reversal lasts about 2h.

Absolute returns show power-law decaying autocorrelation (slope -1.17 in Period 1, -1.07 in Period 2) below about 100 minutes, with a small non-zero level (about 0.002) beyond 200 minutes. Volatility has long memory (Sec 5.2 p.13).

Fat tails: tail slope 3.95±0.18 and 4.04±0.12; q-Gaussian with q≈1.50-1.57 (Sec 5.1 p.9-10). After detrending with a 1-week moving average, the return distributions collapse onto q=1.51 (Sec 5.3 p.15). The series is multifractal; the detrended fluctuation analysis gives H≈0.46-0.48 (Figs 8-9 p.16-18; Table 1 p.20).
papers.evidence_quality: Descriptive and in-sample only: no forecasts, no trading, no costs. The venue is a Reuters composite, not Binance, and the data ends May 2022. Exponents are fitted on raw USD price differences over periods when BTC's price changed several-fold. That likely inflates the long-interval H>0.5; the detrended fluctuation analysis gives H≈0.46-0.48. So the paper's 'trending up to 5 hours' claim is weak and should not be read as contradicting our Binance walk-forward evidence of 1h reversal. No confidence intervals are given for the autocorrelation values. The useful parts are qualitative: short-horizon anti-persistence that is fading over time, and long-memory volatility.

ideas.idea: Record a trailing 168h variance ratio for every hour, VR = Var(2h log returns) / (2 × Var(1h log returns)), with VR<1 meaning anti-persistent. Optionally add a 10-minute-to-1h version. Then test whether the Hourly Mean Reversion hit rate is higher when VR<1 than when VR≥1.
ideas.expected_effect: A live, cheap read on whether the anti-persistent regime the strategy relies on is present or fading. It could explain part of the 2.4 pts/yr decay. Expect a small difference.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Not on the tried list. It may overlap if the Qlib-style factor set already included return-autocorrelation features, which failed as filters.
ideas.citation: 2402.11930 Sec 5.1 p.9 (short-interval H 0.415→0.478); abstract p.1 (moving toward efficiency); Table 1 p.20

ideas.idea: Resting post-only bids on Hourly Mean Reversion signals may mostly fill on losing hours. If part of the reversal starts in the first minutes of hour H, Polymarket moves toward our side and the bid never fills; fills then cluster in hours where price moves against us. In paper and live, log fill/no-fill, time to fill and mid at fill for every resting order, and settle unfilled orders as would-have bets. Compare hit rates of filled vs unfilled. Paper-mode maker fills should also require trades or the book to actually reach our price, or paper results will look better than live.
ideas.expected_effect: The maker hit rate is likely below the 57.3% all-signal rate. This tells us whether the maker 50% break-even is a real advantage over pay-the-ask before the order-style choice is used.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Different from the 'last-15-minute flow' filter that was tried and failed: that screened pre-open flow, while this is about which orders fill after the open.
ideas.citation: 2402.11930 Sec 5.2 p.13 and Sec 6 p.20-21 (negative autocorrelation at short lags, oscillating to about 200 min); 2606.00060 p.7 (its cost model ignores maker/taker routing and partial fills)

ideas.idea: Before recording Kronos forecast spread as a move-size factor, compare it to a multi-horizon volatility forecast (HAR-style mix of last-1h, 24h and 168h realised volatility, using a robust measure such as high-low range because tails are fat), not just a 24h average. Volatility has long memory, so a 24h average is too easy a benchmark.
ideas.expected_effect: Kronos's small advantage on move size may disappear. If so, the cheaper HAR volatility should be the recorded size factor instead of running Kronos for it.
ideas.citation: 2402.11930 Sec 5.2 p.13 (power-law decay of |return| autocorrelation, memory past 200 min); Sec 5.1 p.9-10 (tail slope about 4, q≈1.5)

papers.title: The Negative Drift of a Limit Order Fill (DeLise, 2024)
key_findings: Mechanism (Sec 3, eq.3, p.11): a buy order resting at the best bid always fills when price ticks down, but only sometimes when price stays or rises, so E[mid move | fill] = (Rf*P(U) - P(D)) / P(f), which is negative whenever Rf < 1 and P(U) = P(D).

Calibration on 10Y Treasury futures (TY), 1-second intervals, 20,743 intervals: P(U)=P(D)=0.0173, P(M)=0.965, non-adverse fill rate Rf=0.018 per interval, fill probability on an adverse tick P(f|D)=0.99 (Table 1, p.20).

Drift after a fill: -0.48 ticks in theory, -0.45 ticks measured (Table 2, p.20). In the live TT simulator run (Nov 21 2023, 6AM-1PM EST, 1,683 orders, 521 fills sampled per side), the average drift over the 100 events after a fill was -0.0065 against a 0.015625 tick. That is about 0.42 tick, roughly the half-tick a market order pays (p.16).

About 1/3 of orders never filled. Unfilled orders cluster where price moved away in the favorable direction. The paper says the fill rate when a prediction is right is much lower than when it is wrong (p.7, p.19).

Fill-model comparison vs the TT live baseline (Nov 30 2023, 8AM-5PM, 576,670 events). Fill on every opposite market order: 85% fill rate and badly inflated P&L. Exponential fills: 30%. Always fill on adverse ticks plus a Bernoulli rate otherwise: 65%, closest to the live 60% (Table 5, p.23). All models were calibrated and tested on the same day (p.21).
Short-term alpha signals (order flow, ML, Markov) correlate only 15-25% with the next move, so they cannot dodge most adverse fills (p.26).
papers.evidence_quality: The mechanism is general and holds for any limit order book where price moves through resting orders, including Polymarket's CLOB. The numbers come from one futures contract (TY), a 1-tick-wide and very slow market (price unchanged in 96.5% of 1s intervals). The data is two single days of simulator fills, not real fills, though the author says they closely match live orders. There are no fees, no out-of-sample test (calibration is explicitly in-sample), and no significance tests. The magnitude does not transfer: Polymarket's hourly Up price can jump several 1c ticks within seconds when BTC moves, so the adverse move after a fill is likely larger than half a tick. That is our inference, not the paper's.

ideas.idea: Before offering the resting post-only buy, run a fill-selection test on historical Binance BTCUSDT 1m klines for every past signal: the Mean Reversion walk-forward (620) and held-out (220) bets, and the Kronos bets from the 500-hour backtest. Mark a bet 'resting order would fill' if, in the first two 1m candles of hour H, BTC moved against the bet side enough to push our token down at least one 1c tick. Use the high vs the hour open for Down bets and the low vs the open for Up bets. Near 50c with roughly 0.5-0.6% hourly BTC volatility, one tick is about a 0.012-0.015% BTC move (our estimate). Compare win rates for the would-fill, would-miss and all-bets groups. A resting order's value per filled share is roughly (win rate among would-fill bets) minus (the bid we would pay).
ideas.expected_effect: The paper's mechanism predicts the would-fill group wins less often and the would-miss group more often than the full sample. For Mean Reversion (bets against H-1), the would-fill hours are exactly those where H-1's direction keeps going right after the open, which may be hours where the reversal is failing. If would-fill win rate stays near 57%, resting saves about 2.25c/share vs paying the ask. If it falls to about 50-51% or lower, resting loses despite zero fees. The size is unknown until measured.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Contradicts the planning assumption that a resting order that fills breaks even at 50%. That assumption treats fills as independent of price moves; the paper shows fills are concentrated in adverse moves.
ideas.citation: 2407.16527 Sec 3 eq.3 p.11; Sec 2 p.7; Sec 4 p.16 and p.19; Table 2 p.20

ideas.idea: Paper-mode fill rule for resting orders, adapted from the paper's technique 3. A resting buy at price p fills for sure when our token trades through p (best ask drops to <= p, or a trade prints below p). A fill at exactly p is allowed only after volume traded at p since we posted exceeds the displayed size that was ahead of us at post time. A mere touch never fills. Tag each paper fill as 'trade-through' or 'at-price'.
ideas.expected_effect: Stops paper mode from overstating resting-order fill rate and P&L. In the paper's test, the naive 'fill on next opposite order' rule gave 85% fills and a P&L far above live, versus 60% live. The adverse-fill rule gave 65% and tracked live P&L closely. Needed so paper and live resting-order results stay comparable.

ideas.idea: For every order (both styles), record: order style, time to fill, fill type (trade-through vs at-price), signed Binance BTC move from hour open to fill time relative to the bet, our token's mid at fill and at +30s and +120s, and the final outcome. For resting orders that never fill, also record what the bet would have returned if entered at the ask at the open.
ideas.expected_effect: Measures the negative drift directly on the hourly BTC market, per strategy and order style. Filled resting orders should show a negative short-horizon markout and an adverse BTC move before the fill. This also checks the historical proxy test against real Polymarket fills.
ideas.citation: 2407.16527 Sec 4 p.16 (drift measured over 100 events after each fill), Table 2 p.20

ideas.idea: The per-strategy results panel must show resting-order signals that did not fill, with their would-be outcome at the ask. Keep filled-bet accuracy separate from signal accuracy on all signals.
ideas.expected_effect: Without this, resting-order results will show lower win rates that look like the strategy getting worse, when the cause is that execution filtered out the favorable hours. The paper found unfilled orders are concentrated where price moved favorably, with about 1/3 of orders unfilled.

papers.title: Fragmentation, Price Formation, and Cross-Impact in Bitcoin Markets (Albers, Cucuringu, Howison, Shestopaloff, 2021)
key_findings: Data: the 14 most liquid BTC markets in Feb 2021 (11 perps, 2 quarterly futures, 1 spot), websocket order book snapshots and trades resampled to 50ms. Training Feb 22-27 2021, out-of-sample test Feb 28-Mar 1 2021 (pp.1, 7-8, 23).
Linear models explain 10-37% of the variation in 500ms future returns. Out-of-sample R2 is about 91% of in-sample at 500ms (Table 5, p.29). Every horizon studied is sub-second to 1 second.
Binance and Huobi perps/futures lead price formation; Bybit, FTX and Bitmex lag (pp.21-22, p.49). The best pair: FTX's next 500ms predicted from Binance USDT perp features alone, R2 25.9% (p.21).

Taker fees in the study are 1.5-7.5 bps at VIP tier and 4-7.5 bps at default tier (Table 2, p.8). At default fees, every single-market taker strategy lost (average -18,899 bps over the 2 test days) (p.25). The cross-market models also lost on all 14 markets at default fees, and 4 of 14 made money at VIP fees (Table 6, pp.30-31).

Fee-regime argument: high taker fees (plus high maker rebates) predispose a venue to lag, and a lag only pays if it exceeds what the fees imply (pp.27-28). Price gaps between venues can sit inside a no-arbitrage band as wide as the combined taker fees (p.14).
The flow-to-return relation at 500ms saturates at extremes (sigmoid shape). The authors guess extreme flow comes from less-informed traders or forced liquidations (p.16).

Live maker test on the Bybit BTC perp, Jul 8-13 2021, more than 4 months after calibration: 1.537M USD filled, round trips lost -4.47 bps before rebates and made +0.53 bps after the 5 bps round-trip rebate. The never-cancel benchmark lost -6.82 bps (run Jul 17-18 with $100 orders). Median time between opposite fills: 328s vs 27s (p.47).

Adverse selection on maker fills grows with horizon. Cancel-rule bot averages: -0.51 bps at 0.5s, -1.99 at 60s, -2.44 at 300s, -2.88 at 1200s. Never-cancel benchmark: -0.49, -2.94, -3.26, -3.16. The benchmark is about 1 bp worse after about 10s (Tables 15-16, pp.48-49).
Maker strategies could not be backtested because queue position cannot be tracked from order book snapshots without per-order data (Sec 6.1, pp.43-45).
papers.evidence_quality: Horizon mismatch is severe: 500ms-1s prediction vs our 1-hour hold. The out-of-sample test covers only 2 days in Feb 2021, and several venues no longer exist (FTX) or have changed. Taker P&L assumes fills at top-of-book prices, where sizes are often tiny, and fees are included. The live maker test is real money but short (about 5.4 days) on one venue. The benchmark ran at a different time with 20x smaller orders, so the comparison is not side by side, and no significance is reported. The +0.53 bps profit exists only because of a 5 bps rebate, which Polymarket makers do not get. Nothing here is measured on binary or prediction markets. What transfers is the fee-regime lag argument, the result that adverse selection on resting fills grows with horizon, and the warning that maker backtests are unreliable.

ideas.idea: Answer the open question directly. For every hour (not just signal hours), log Polymarket Up best bid, best ask and mid at t = 0, 15, 60 and 120s after the open, together with H-1's direction, spot fz, perp fz, CLV and Kronos P(up). Measure the lean (Up mid minus 0.50) against H-1's direction across all hours and in Mean Reversion signal hours. The paper's fee-regime argument gives a reason Polymarket could lag or hold a biased price. Its taker cost at 50c is about 1.75c fee plus 0.5c half-spread, around 450 bps of the token price, versus 1.5-7.5 bps for the perps studied. Prices can sit inside a band that wide without being arbitraged.
ideas.expected_effect: This decides whether the 57.3% hit rate is an edge against the price actually paid. If the open price already leans against H-1 by about the size of Mean Reversion's edge (about 5-7c) on signal hours, paying the ask has no edge. If the lean is about zero, the 57.3% vs 52.25% break-even comparison holds. The paper provides no Polymarket evidence, only the mechanism. About 720 hours/month give a usable lean estimate within weeks, while signal-hour estimates will be slow (about 20/month).
ideas.citation: 2108.09750 Sec 3.1.4 p.14 (no-arbitrage band); Sec 4.2 pp.27-28 (fee regime and lag); Table 2 p.8

ideas.idea: If the resting order style ships, test a cancel-and-skip rule during the 120s entry window: cancel the unfilled resting order if Binance BTC moves against the bet by more than k, with k set to a move worth about 2c of our token's price. Do not re-enter; the direction is still decided once at the open. First evaluate it in the historical 1m/1s kline simulation from the DeLise fill-selection test, assuming 1-2s cancel latency.
ideas.expected_effect: Fewer adverse fills and fewer fills overall. In the paper, the cancel rule improved round trips from -6.82 to -4.47 bps and cut adverse selection by about 1 bp after 10s. But the bot was colocated with sub-1ms latency and still saw adverse selection grow to about -2.9 bps at 20-40 minutes, and it was profitable only because of a 5 bps rebate. On Polymarket, with no maker rebate and pickers who also watch Binance, the rule must beat the ~2.25c pay-the-ask cost on its own. Sharp moves will still pick us off before the cancel lands.
ideas.citation: 2108.09750 Sec 6.1 pp.40-43 (cancel criterion); Sec 6.3 p.47; Tables 15-16 pp.48-49

ideas.idea: Treat paper-mode resting-order P&L as an upper bound until it is checked against live fills. If our Polymarket feed only shows total size per price level with no per-order IDs (check the feed), queue position after cancellations cannot be known, so at-price paper fills are guesses. Calibrate the at-price fill rate from a stretch of live minimum-size (5-share) resting orders before comparing order styles on the panel.
ideas.expected_effect: Stops a paper-only comparison from wrongly favoring the resting style. The authors judged maker backtests on snapshot data 'virtually impossible' and tested live instead. This overlaps with the DeLise fill-rule idea.

ideas.idea: Record, for each Mean Reversion bet, the H-1 spot fz magnitude bucket (1.2-1.5, 1.5-2, 2-3, >3) and the liquidation notional on the push side as a share of H-1 taker volume on that side. Show win rate by bucket on the panel, as observation only, not a filter.
ideas.expected_effect: The paper sees price impact saturate at extreme flow and guesses extreme flow comes from less-informed traders or forced liquidations. If that holds at the hourly scale, reversals should be stronger after liquidation-heavy or extreme pushes. Transfer from 500ms windows is weak, and at about 20 bets/month each bucket's sample is too small to act on for a long time.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Repeats the planned liquidations context factor; this only sharpens its definition. No fz upper cap has been tested, and bucketing the existing 840 bets risks overfitting the 1.20 threshold.

papers.title: Market Simulation under Adverse Selection (Lalor and Swishchuk, v3 2026)
key_findings: Share of adverse fills for a simple resting-order poster in the TT simulator, one day each, 8:30-16:00 EST: ES 767/941 (81.5%, 2024-04-24), NQ 1,269/1,929 (65.8%, 2024-04-25), CL 518/625 (82.9%, 2024-04-23), ZN 199/224 (88.8%, 2024-04-24) (Table 2, p.7). Order spacing was 4 ticks for ES and CL, 16 for NQ and 1 for ZN, so not strictly at the touch (p.6).

A fill is called adverse when an order fills at the bid and the next new bid is lower, or at the ask and the next new ask is higher (pp.6-7). When price moves through a resting level, the fill is mechanically certain (p.4).

Simulators that generate market orders independently of price moves, or that don't force fills when price crosses a level, under-count adverse fills. The authors say this gets worse at finer time steps (p.4).

The non-adverse fill probability was set heuristically at 0.2 to reproduce Table 2. The authors say there is 'no well-established or robust method' to calibrate it (p.11, p.13). CL simulation over 330 runs of 120 seconds: 3,950 ask and 3,943 bid fills adverse, vs 825 and 813 non-adverse (Table 4, p.15). ES, NQ and ZN counts in Table 5, p.23.

The strategy did 'much worse' in the improved simulator, but P&L appears only as histograms with no numbers (pp.16-17). The authors say ZN's non-adverse fill probability should be much lower because its queues are larger (p.23).
papers.evidence_quality: Weak and largely repeats DeLise, which it cites, using the same TT simulator setup. Each contract gets one day of simulated fills, not real ones. There are no fees, no out-of-sample test and no numeric P&L. The 0.2 fill probability was chosen to match the same data it is then checked against, so the check is circular. There is a date inconsistency: the Table 4 caption says April 24th, 2025 while the data elsewhere is 2024 (p.15). The venues are CME futures on a 120-second market-making horizon. The only new practical point for us is the warning about snapshot sampling.

ideas.idea: In the paper fill simulator, check for fills using every trade and price update between checks, not only the book state at check time. If the engine polls the Polymarket book, keep the lowest best ask (for our buy) and the lowest trade price seen since the last poll. Any trade-through of our resting price during that interval counts as a fill at our price, even if the price has recovered by the next snapshot.
ideas.expected_effect: Prevents paper mode from missing exactly the adverse fills that matter: brief dips through our bid during a fast BTC move in the 120s window. Missing them would make the resting style look safer than it is.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Repeats the trade-through rule from the DeLise fill-rule idea; this is the sampling detail needed to implement it correctly.

ideas.idea: Do not borrow a constant non-adverse fill probability (such as 0.2) from futures studies for Polymarket paper fills. Estimate the adverse vs at-price fill mix only from our own resting orders, split by fill type and by how fast BTC was moving in the entry window.
ideas.expected_effect: Avoids a made-up fill rate driving the paper comparison of order styles. The adverse share in this paper ranged from 66% to 89% across contracts and order spacings, and the authors admit the 0.2 value has no robust calibration.
ideas.conflicts_with_what_we_tried: Repeats the per-order recording idea from DeLise; adds only the warning against importing a fixed fill rate.
ideas.citation: 2409.12721 Table 2 p.7; Sec 4 p.11; Sec 5 p.13 and Table 4 p.15
